Board-pattern tables

Fast differential frameworks for common board stems.

Vomiting in infants: fastest discriminators

BiliousMalrotation/volvulus or distal obstruction until proven otherwise.
Projectile, nonbilious, 2–8 wkPyloric stenosis.
Episodic pain + lethargyIntussusception.
Delayed meconium + distentionHirschsprung disease or another distal obstruction.

Neonatal metabolic crisis

Hyperammonemia + respiratory alkalosisUrea-cycle disorder.
Hyperammonemia + anion-gap acidosis/ketosisOrganic acidemia.
Hypoketotic hypoglycemia during fasting/illnessFatty-acid oxidation defect.
Liver failure + succinylacetoneTyrosinemia type 1.
Ill after milk feeds + liver dysfunction/E coliGalactosemia.

Nephritic vs nephrotic

NephriticHematuria/RBC casts, hypertension, edema, reduced GFR; think PSGN, IgA disease, lupus.
NephroticHeavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, edema, hyperlipidemia; minimal-change disease is most common in children.

Abdominal mass in a child

Smooth renal mass, usually unilateralWilms tumor.
Irregular mass crossing midline + catecholamine metabolitesNeuroblastoma.
Rapidly enlarging ileocecal/abdominal massBurkitt lymphoma.
Sausage-shaped mass + episodic painIntussusception.

Immunodeficiency pattern recognition

Thrush/diarrhea/opportunistic infection in early infancySCID.
Boy, recurrent bacterial infections after 6 mo, absent tonsilsX-linked agammaglobulinemia.
Catalase-positive infections/granulomasCGD.
Eczema + infections + small plateletsWiskott-Aldrich.
Conotruncal defect + hypocalcemia + T-cell defectDiGeorge.

Hip pain by age/pattern

Infant, unstable/dislocated hipDevelopmental dysplasia.
Young child, limp + avascular necrosisLegg-Calvé-Perthes.
Overweight adolescent, knee/hip pain + loss of internal rotationSCFE.
Toxic child, exquisite ROM painSeptic arthritis.

Microcytic anemia: first split

Low ferritin + high RDWIron deficiency.
Very low MCV + relatively preserved/high RBC countThalassemia trait.
Basophilic stippling/exposure historyConsider lead toxicity.

Pediatric “do not miss” eye findings

LeukocoriaRetinoblastoma until proven otherwise.
Pain with EOM/proptosis/vision changeOrbital cellulitis.
Absent red reflex in newbornUrgent ophthalmologic evaluation for cataract/retinal pathology.

Growth patterns

SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Growth & Development

Growth faltering: pattern recognition

PatternWeight usually falls first; length is affected with more prolonged/severe undernutrition, and head circumference is generally preserved until late.
HistoryClarify caloric intake, feeding technique, vomiting/diarrhea, restrictive diets, food insecurity, chronic disease symptoms, and psychosocial stressors.
Red flagsDevelopmental regression, organomegaly, persistent respiratory/GI symptoms, dysmorphism, or poor linear growth should broaden the workup beyond inadequate intake.
Board pearlA well-appearing child with isolated poor weight gain most often needs a careful feeding history before an extensive laboratory evaluation.
SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Growth & Development

Short stature: common board distinctions

FamilialShort parents, normal growth velocity, bone age roughly matches chronologic age.
Constitutional delayDelayed bone age, otherwise normal growth velocity, delayed puberty, and often a family history of late bloomers.
Pathologic clueFalling growth velocity or disproportionate loss of height percentile suggests endocrine, systemic, nutritional, or genetic disease.
Board pearlGrowth velocity and bone age are more informative than a single height percentile.
SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Growth & Development

Growth velocity: use the trajectory

WeightWeight is the most sensitive early marker of inadequate caloric intake.
Length/heightPoor linear growth or falling height velocity raises concern for chronic systemic, nutritional, endocrine, or genetic disease.
Head circumferenceDisproportionate microcephaly or macrocephaly should be interpreted with parental head size, growth trajectory, and neurologic development.
Board pearl A single percentile is less useful than the direction and velocity of growth over time.
CLINICAL CLUSTER

Developmental surveillance

SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Growth & Development

Developmental milestone red flags

Always abnormalLoss of previously acquired skills at any age.
MotorPersistent head lag around 4 months, inability to sit independently by about 9 months, or clear early hand preference before ~18 months should prompt evaluation.
Language/socialFailure to progress in communication or social reciprocity should trigger hearing assessment and developmental screening rather than “watchful waiting” when concerns are substantial.
Board pearl Milestone ranges are broad, but regression and loss of skills are never normal developmental variants.

CLINICAL CLUSTER

Developmental delay & regression

SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Development

Developmental regression

DefinitionLoss of previously acquired skills is abnormal and should not be attributed to normal developmental variation.
Think broadlyNeurodegenerative/metabolic disease, epileptic encephalopathy, neuromuscular disease, severe psychosocial deprivation, or progressive CNS pathology.
ApproachConfirm true loss of skills, identify the developmental domains involved, and look for seizures, weakness, vision/hearing change, organomegaly, or episodic decompensation.
Board pearlDelay can be static; regression implies a progressive process until proven otherwise.
SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Development

Intellectual disability: diagnostic frame

DefinitionDeficits in intellectual function plus adaptive functioning with onset during the developmental period.
EvaluationConfirm hearing/vision, review prenatal/perinatal exposures and family history, examine for dysmorphism or neurologic findings, and pursue genetic/metabolic testing when indicated.
ClueGlobal developmental delay in a young child is a developmental diagnosis; intellectual disability is assigned when formal cognitive/adaptive assessment is appropriate.
Board pearl The degree of adaptive impairment—not IQ alone—determines severity in current diagnostic frameworks.
CLINICAL CLUSTER

Neurodevelopmental syndromes

SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Development

Rett syndrome

PatternGirls with apparently normal early development followed by regression, loss of purposeful hand use, stereotypic hand movements, and acquired microcephaly.
GeneUsually MECP2-related and X-linked dominant; most cases are de novo.
AssociatedSeizures, gait abnormalities, breathing irregularities, and scoliosis may develop.
Board pearl A girl who develops normally and then loses language/hand skills with hand stereotypies is a classic Rett pattern.

    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Jaundice & cholestasis

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Neonatology

    Neonatal jaundice: red flags

    Concerning timingJaundice in the first 24 hours of life is pathologic until proven otherwise.
    Conjugated bilirubinDirect/conjugated hyperbilirubinemia is never physiologic and warrants evaluation for cholestasis.
    Hemolysis cluesAnemia, reticulocytosis, rapid bilirubin rise, positive DAT, or blood-group incompatibility.
    Cholestasis cluesDark urine, pale/acholic stools, hepatomegaly, poor growth, or persistent jaundice.
    Board pearlThe board split is usually unconjugated hemolysis/physiologic jaundice versus conjugated cholestasis.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Neonatology

    Neonatal cholestasis: do not miss biliary atresia

    RecognizePersistent jaundice with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, dark urine, pale/acholic stools, and hepatomegaly.
    Why urgentBiliary atresia requires rapid evaluation because earlier surgical drainage improves outcomes.
    DifferentialInfection, metabolic/genetic liver disease, endocrine disease, parenteral nutrition, and anatomic obstruction.
    Board pearlAcholic stool in a jaundiced infant is a high-yield clue to obstructive cholestasis.
    COMPARE / CONTRAST

    Neonatal jaundice: compare the common patterns

    PhysiologicBegins after first 24 h, peaks over first several days, then resolves.
    Breastfeeding jaundiceEarly; inadequate intake/dehydration with low milk transfer.
    Breast-milk jaundiceLater/persistent unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia in an otherwise thriving breastfed infant.
    PathologicFirst 24 h, rapid rise, significant direct hyperbilirubinemia, anemia/illness, or prolonged course with red flags.
    Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia is never physiologic.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Prematurity & respiratory disease

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Neonatology

    Respiratory distress syndrome vs transient tachypnea

    RDSPrematurity + surfactant deficiency; diffuse reticulogranular/ground-glass appearance and air bronchograms. Support with CPAP/oxygen and surfactant when indicated.
    TTNUsually term/late-preterm, often after cesarean delivery; delayed fetal lung-fluid clearance with tachypnea that improves over the first 1–3 days.
    DistinctionRDS is strongly linked to prematurity and surfactant deficiency; TTN is a transient fluid-clearance problem.
    Board pearlA preterm infant who worsens after birth points toward RDS; a vigorous term infant after C-section who rapidly improves points toward TTN.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Neonatology

    Apnea of prematurity

    DefinitionRecurrent pauses in breathing in a premature infant due to immature respiratory control, often with bradycardia and/or desaturation.
    Exclude firstInfection, hypoglycemia, anemia, temperature instability, seizures, medication effects, and airway/lung disease.
    TreatmentSupportive measures and methylxanthine therapy (commonly caffeine) for clinically significant recurrent episodes.
    Board pearl New or worsening apnea in a preterm infant is not automatically “apnea of prematurity”—look for an acute trigger.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Neonatology

    Bronchopulmonary dysplasia

    WhoPrimarily very preterm infants with prolonged oxygen/ventilatory exposure and immature lungs.
    PatternPersistent oxygen requirement or respiratory support with chronic tachypnea, retractions, and poor growth.
    Long termHigher risk of respiratory infections, reactive airway symptoms, pulmonary hypertension, and neurodevelopmental complications.
    Board pearl Think BPD when a very preterm infant continues to need respiratory support well beyond the acute RDS period.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Neonatal infection

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Neonatology

    Neonatal sepsis: practical pattern

    PresentationTemperature instability, poor feeding, lethargy, respiratory distress, apnea, hypotension, or glucose instability may be the only clues.
    Early-onset organismsGroup B Streptococcus and gram-negative enteric organisms, especially E coli, are classic.
    ActionA sick neonate warrants prompt cultures and empiric parenteral antibiotics; do not wait for a focal source.
    Board pearlNeonates often show nonspecific deterioration rather than a classic adult sepsis picture.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Neonatology

    Neonatal herpes simplex virus

    TimingOften presents in the first weeks of life; maternal history of genital lesions may be absent.
    FormsSkin/eye/mouth disease, CNS disease, or disseminated disease with hepatitis, shock, and coagulopathy.
    ActionObtain appropriate HSV testing and start IV acyclovir promptly when neonatal HSV is strongly suspected.
    Board pearl Vesicles are helpful when present, but neonatal HSV can present as sepsis, hepatitis, or encephalitis without a rash.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Metabolic & feeding problems

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Neonatology

    Neonatal hypoglycemia: who is at risk?

    Risk groupsInfants of diabetic mothers, small- or large-for-gestational-age infants, preterm infants, and sick/stressed newborns.
    SymptomsJitteriness, poor feeding, lethargy, apnea, cyanosis, temperature instability, or seizures; many infants are asymptomatic.
    ApproachEarly feeding is appropriate for many asymptomatic at-risk infants; symptomatic or persistent/severe hypoglycemia requires prompt glucose therapy and evaluation for an underlying cause.
    Board pearl Treat the symptomatic newborn, not just the number—neurologic symptoms with low glucose are an emergency.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    GI emergency

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Neonatology

    Necrotizing enterocolitis

    WhoMost often premature infants after enteral feeding has begun.
    RecognizeFeeding intolerance, abdominal distention/tenderness, emesis, bloody stool, temperature instability, or apnea.
    ImagingPneumatosis intestinalis is classic; portal venous gas or free air suggests advanced disease/perforation.
    ManagementStop feeds, gastric decompression, IV fluids/nutrition, broad-spectrum antibiotics, serial exams/imaging; surgery for perforation or necrotic bowel.
    Board pearlPremature infant + abdominal distention + bloody stool + pneumatosis = NEC.

    Adolescent Medicine

    5 snapshots · 1 comparisons · 188 unique facts
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Puberty & amenorrhea

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Adolescent Medicine

    Delayed puberty: first split

    BoysNo testicular enlargement by ~14 years is a typical threshold for evaluation.
    GirlsNo breast development by ~13 years or failure to progress through puberty warrants evaluation.
    PatternConstitutional delay usually has delayed bone age and otherwise normal growth velocity; hypergonadotropic states have elevated gonadotropins, whereas central causes have low/inappropriately normal gonadotropins.
    Board pearl Bone age plus gonadotropin pattern quickly separates constitutional delay from primary gonadal failure and central causes.
    COMPARE / CONTRAST

    Primary amenorrhea: uterus present vs absent

    Uterus present + no secondary sex traitsConsider gonadal dysgenesis or central hypogonadism.
    Uterus present + secondary sex traitsConsider outflow obstruction or less commonly endocrine causes.
    Uterus absent + normal breastsThink Müllerian agenesis vs androgen insensitivity; pubic/axillary hair helps distinguish them.
    Pelvic anatomy is the fastest first branch. When pregnancy is biologically possible, pregnancy testing still belongs in the evaluation.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Reproductive health

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Adolescent Medicine

    Estrogen-containing contraception: major contraindication patterns

    Thrombosis riskPrior thromboembolism or major thrombophilia can make estrogen unsafe.
    NeurologicMigraine with aura is a key contraindication because of ischemic stroke risk.
    OtherActive breast cancer and significant liver disease are important contraindication categories.
    Board pearl When a vignette emphasizes clot risk or migraine with aura, avoid estrogen-containing contraception.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Nutrition & medical instability

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Adolescent Medicine

    Eating-disorder medical instability

    Red flagsBradycardia, hypotension/orthostasis, hypothermia, dehydration, syncope, electrolyte abnormalities, or significant ECG changes.
    Refeeding riskSeverely malnourished patients are at risk for electrolyte shifts, especially hypophosphatemia, during nutritional rehabilitation.
    PrincipleMedical stabilization and nutritional restoration come before psychotherapy alone when physiologic instability is present.
    Board pearlIn a medically unstable adolescent with restrictive eating, the immediate issue is physiologic stabilization—not weight counseling.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Confidentiality & preventive care

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Adolescent Medicine

    Adolescent confidentiality: limits

    DefaultProvide private time with adolescents and explain confidentiality clearly.
    Break confidentialitySafety overrides confidentiality when there is suspected abuse, imminent risk of serious self-harm/harm to others, or other legally mandated reporting circumstances.
    CommunicationWhenever feasible, tell the adolescent what must be disclosed and involve them in how disclosure occurs.
    Board pearl Confidentiality is the rule; imminent safety threats and mandatory reporting are the major exceptions.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Breast concerns

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Adolescent Medicine

    Adolescent breast mass

    Most commonFibroadenoma—mobile, rubbery, well-circumscribed mass.
    ImagingUltrasound is the preferred initial imaging test for a persistent or concerning adolescent breast mass.
    EscalateRapid growth, very large size, fixation, skin/nipple changes, or atypical imaging warrants surgical evaluation.
    Board pearl Most adolescent breast masses are benign; fibroadenoma is the classic board answer.

    Immunization & postexposure prevention

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Preventive Pediatrics

    Live vaccines: major contraindications

    AvoidSevere immunodeficiency and pregnancy are major contraindications to live-attenuated vaccines.
    ExamplesMMR, varicella, intranasal influenza, and rotavirus are live vaccines.
    Not contraindicationsMild acute illness, antibiotic use, breastfeeding, and most household exposure situations are not reasons to delay routine vaccination.
    Board pearlKnow the true contraindications; boards often test common false contraindications.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Preventive Pediatrics

    Rotavirus vaccine: key contraindications

    Do not giveHistory of intussusception or severe combined immunodeficiency.
    WhyBoth conditions carry an unacceptable risk profile for live oral rotavirus vaccination.
    PearlA small intussusception risk after vaccination does not outweigh the benefit in otherwise eligible infants.
    Board pearlPrior intussusception is an absolute contraindication to rotavirus vaccination.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Preventive Pediatrics

    Measles postexposure prophylaxis

    MMRFor susceptible vaccine-eligible contacts, MMR within 72 hours can prevent or modify disease.
    Infants 6–11 monthsMMR may be used after exposure/outbreak; this early dose does not count toward the routine 2-dose series. MMRV is not used before 12 months.
    Immune globulinUse within 6 days for selected susceptible high-risk contacts, especially young infants, pregnant people without immunity, and severely immunocompromised patients.
    Board pearlDocumented measles immunity means postexposure prophylaxis is not needed.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Preventive Pediatrics

    Meningococcal vaccination: high-risk clues

    RoutineAdolescents receive routine MenACWY vaccination with a later booster according to the current schedule.
    Earlier/high riskFunctional/anatomic asplenia and persistent complement deficiencies warrant earlier vaccination and ongoing boosters.
    ExposureVaccination does not replace antibiotic chemoprophylaxis after a qualifying close meningococcal exposure.
    Board pearl Asplenia and terminal complement deficiency are the classic reasons to think “meningococcus” both for infection risk and vaccination.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Screening & anticipatory guidance

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Preventive Pediatrics

    Newborn screening: the bedside triad

    HearingUniversal newborn hearing screening; failed screens require timely diagnostic audiology.
    CCHDPulse-oximetry screening identifies critical congenital heart disease that may not be obvious on exam.
    MetabolicState newborn screens detect selected endocrine, metabolic, hematologic, and other disorders before symptoms develop.
    Board pearl A “normal newborn exam” does not replace hearing, CCHD, and state metabolic screening.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Preventive Pediatrics

    Lead exposure

    PresentationMost children with elevated lead levels are asymptomatic.
    EffectsDevelopmental/behavioral problems, learning difficulty, abdominal symptoms, anemia, and severe neurologic toxicity can occur with greater exposure.
    Management frameConfirm elevated screening values when required, identify/remove the exposure source, optimize iron/calcium nutrition, and use chelation only for sufficiently high levels or severe toxicity.
    Board pearl Because lead toxicity is often silent, risk-based or recommended screening matters more than waiting for symptoms.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Preventive Pediatrics

    Safe sleep and SIDS risk reduction

    PositionPlace infants supine for every sleep.
    EnvironmentUse a firm, flat sleep surface without loose bedding, pillows, positioners, or soft objects.
    AvoidSmoke exposure and overheating; room-sharing without bed-sharing is preferred.
    Board pearl Back to sleep on a firm, empty surface is the core SIDS-prevention message.

    Genetics & Dysmorphology

    11 snapshots · 1 comparisons · 195 unique facts
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Chromosomal & phenotypic syndromes

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Genetics & Dysmorphology

    Down syndrome: board associations

    CardiacAtrioventricular septal defects are classic; VSD/ASD can also occur.
    GIDuodenal atresia and Hirschsprung disease are important associations.
    HematologyTransient abnormal myelopoiesis and increased leukemia risk.
    OtherHypothyroidism, hearing/vision problems, obstructive sleep apnea, and atlantoaxial instability.
    Board pearlDown syndrome questions often test a complication rather than the diagnosis itself.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Genetics & Dysmorphology

    Turner syndrome

    Core45,X or mosaic monosomy X; short stature and gonadal dysgenesis with hypergonadotropic hypogonadism.
    CardiacCoarctation of the aorta and bicuspid aortic valve.
    Renal/otherHorseshoe kidney, lymphedema, webbed neck, and increased autoimmune thyroid disease risk.
    Board pearlShort girl + delayed puberty + coarctation = Turner syndrome until proven otherwise.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Genetics & Dysmorphology

    Noonan syndrome

    PhenotypeShort stature, webbed neck, hypertelorism/low-set ears, pectus deformity, and possible lymphedema.
    HeartPulmonary valve stenosis is classic; hypertrophic cardiomyopathy can also occur.
    GeneticsRAS/MAPK pathway; PTPN11 is the most common gene, with SOS1 and RAF1 among other causes.
    BleedingFactor XI deficiency and other coagulation/platelet abnormalities can cause easy bruising or prolonged bleeding.
    Board pearlNoonan resembles Turner phenotypically but occurs in both sexes and usually has a normal karyotype.
    COMPARE / CONTRAST

    Turner vs Noonan syndrome

    Turner45,X; phenotypic female; short stature, webbed neck, lymphedema, streak ovaries, coarctation/bicuspid aortic valve.
    NoonanUsually RAS/MAPK-pathway mutation; affects either sex; short stature, webbed neck, pectus deformity, pulmonic stenosis/HCM, bleeding diathesis.
    SharedShort stature, neck webbing, widely spaced nipples/pectus-type chest features can overlap.
    Pulmonic stenosis suggests Noonan; coarctation + gonadal dysgenesis suggests Turner.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Craniosynostosis syndromes

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Genetics & Dysmorphology

    Apert vs Crouzon syndrome

    SharedCraniosynostosis with midface hypoplasia and shallow orbits/proptosis.
    ApertSyndactyly/mitten-hand deformity is the key distinguishing feature; bicoronal synostosis is common.
    CrouzonCraniosynostosis without the characteristic limb syndactyly of Apert.
    Board pearlCraniosynostosis + syndactyly = Apert.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Metabolic dysmorphology

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Genetics & Dysmorphology

    Smith-Lemli-Opitz syndrome

    DefectAutosomal-recessive 7-dehydrocholesterol reductase (DHCR7) deficiency.
    LabsIncreased 7-dehydrocholesterol with decreased cholesterol.
    PhenotypeMicrocephaly, facial anomalies, 2–3 toe syndactyly, postaxial polydactyly, and genital anomalies such as hypospadias/ambiguous genitalia.
    Board pearl2–3 toe syndactyly + genital anomalies + low cholesterol points to Smith-Lemli-Opitz.

    Connective-tissue disorder

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Genetics & Dysmorphology

    Marfan syndrome: what gets tested

    SkeletalTall habitus, long extremities/arachnodactyly, pectus deformity, scoliosis.
    EyeEctopia lentis is characteristic.
    CardiovascularAortic root dilation/aneurysm and mitral valve prolapse are major morbidity drivers.
    Board pearlThe life-threatening issue in Marfan syndrome is progressive aortic root disease.

    Neurodevelopmental genetic syndromes

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Genetics & Dysmorphology

    Fragile X syndrome

    GeneFMR1 CGG-repeat expansion with methylation and reduced FMRP expression.
    PatternIntellectual disability/autism features, long face, large ears, joint laxity, and postpubertal macroorchidism.
    InheritanceX-linked with anticipation related to repeat expansion, especially through maternal transmission.
    Board pearl A boy with developmental delay/autism plus large ears and macroorchidism should trigger Fragile X testing.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Genetics & Dysmorphology

    Williams syndrome

    Genetics7q11.23 deletion involving ELN.
    PatternDistinctive facies, highly social personality, developmental differences, and hypercalcemia.
    CardiacSupravalvular aortic stenosis is the classic lesion.
    Board pearl Hypercalcemia + “cocktail-party” personality + supravalvular aortic stenosis = Williams syndrome.

    Neurocutaneous syndromes

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Genetics & Dysmorphology

    Neurofibromatosis type 1

    HallmarksCafé-au-lait macules, axillary/inguinal freckling, neurofibromas, and Lisch nodules.
    ComplicationsOptic pathway glioma, learning problems, skeletal abnormalities, and hypertension from renal artery stenosis or pheochromocytoma.
    GeneNF1 tumor-suppressor gene; autosomal dominant with variable expression.
    Board pearl Multiple café-au-lait macules plus axillary freckling are a high-yield NF1 combination.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Genetics & Dysmorphology

    Tuberous sclerosis complex

    SkinHypomelanotic “ash-leaf” macules, facial angiofibromas, shagreen patches, and periungual fibromas.
    NeurologicSeizures—including infantile spasms—and developmental/behavioral disorders are common.
    Other organsRenal angiomyolipomas/cysts and cardiac rhabdomyomas are classic associations.
    Board pearl Infantile spasms plus hypopigmented macules should immediately raise concern for tuberous sclerosis.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Overgrowth & tumor-predisposition

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Genetics & Dysmorphology

    Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome

    PatternMacrosomia, macroglossia, omphalocele/abdominal wall defects, hemihyperplasia, and neonatal hypoglycemia.
    Cancer riskIncreased risk of embryonal tumors, especially Wilms tumor and hepatoblastoma.
    Follow-upRequires tumor surveillance in childhood according to current protocols.
    Board pearl Macroglossia + overgrowth + neonatal hypoglycemia is a classic Beckwith-Wiedemann stem.

    Hyperammonemia & nitrogen metabolism

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Metabolic Disorders

    Hyperammonemia: board-pattern approach

    Urea cycle disorderIll neonate after protein feeding with markedly elevated ammonia, usually normal glucose/anion gap/lactate, and often respiratory alkalosis from hyperventilation.
    Organic acidemiaHyperammonemia may occur, but elevated anion-gap metabolic acidosis, ketosis/ketotic hypoglycemia, and sometimes lactic acidosis point away from a primary UCD.
    Fatty-acid oxidation defectThink fasting/illness-triggered hypoketotic hypoglycemia; hyperammonemia may occur.
    Pyruvate metabolism disorderLactic acidosis accompanying hyperammonemia is a useful differentiator from a classic UCD.
    Board pearlNeonatal hyperammonemia + respiratory alkalosis is a classic UCD signal; metabolic acidosis points toward an organic acidemia.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Metabolic Disorders

    Ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency

    InheritanceX-linked urea-cycle disorder.
    LabsHyperammonemia with respiratory alkalosis, low BUN, and elevated urinary orotic acid.
    ClueA previously well neonate who deteriorates after protein feeding without an anion-gap acidosis is a classic presentation.
    Board pearl Hyperammonemia + respiratory alkalosis + elevated urine orotic acid strongly suggests OTC deficiency.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Metabolic Disorders

    Organic acidemia: propionic vs methylmalonic

    Shared patternIll neonate/infant with anion-gap metabolic acidosis, ketosis, poor feeding, vomiting, and possible hyperammonemia.
    MethylmalonicCan be caused by methylmalonyl-CoA mutase defects or cobalamin-related abnormalities; methylmalonic acid is elevated.
    PropionicPropionyl-CoA carboxylase deficiency; propionic acid derivatives accumulate.
    Board pearl Hyperammonemia does not automatically mean a urea-cycle defect—anion-gap acidosis and ketosis point toward an organic acidemia.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Amino-acid & organic metabolism

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Metabolic Disorders

    Hereditary tyrosinemia type 1

    CauseAutosomal-recessive fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase (FAH) deficiency, the final step of tyrosine degradation.
    Diagnostic metaboliteSuccinylacetone in blood or urine; it is also used in newborn screening.
    Liver patternProgressive liver dysfunction with coagulopathy, hepatomegaly/hyperbilirubinemia and hypoglycemia; AFP may be markedly elevated while aminotransferases are only mildly elevated.
    Renal patternProximal tubular dysfunction/Fanconi syndrome with phosphate wasting, aminoaciduria and metabolic acidosis; rickets may result.
    Board pearlSevere infantile liver dysfunction + high AFP + succinylacetone is the high-yield combination.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Metabolic Disorders

    Maple syrup urine disease

    DefectBranched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase deficiency.
    PresentationNeonatal poor feeding, vomiting, lethargy/encephalopathy, abnormal tone, and a characteristic sweet/maple odor.
    Amino acidsLeucine, isoleucine, and valine accumulate.
    Board pearlNeurologic deterioration in the first week of life + sweet odor = MSUD.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Metabolic Disorders

    Phenylketonuria

    DefectUsually phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency causing elevated phenylalanine.
    UntreatedIntellectual disability, seizures, eczema, hypopigmentation, and a musty/mousy odor.
    ManagementRestrict phenylalanine and ensure adequate tyrosine; selected patients benefit from tetrahydrobiopterin therapy.
    Board pearlNewborn screening prevents the classic neurologic phenotype when treatment begins early.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Carbohydrate & energy metabolism

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Metabolic Disorders

    Classic galactosemia

    DefectGalactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase (GALT) deficiency.
    TimingSymptoms begin after breast milk or lactose-containing formula is introduced.
    PresentationVomiting, jaundice/hepatomegaly, hypoglycemia, poor growth, and risk of E coli sepsis.
    ManagementRemove galactose/lactose from the diet.
    Board pearlA sick jaundiced neonate after milk feeds + E coli sepsis is a classic galactosemia stem.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Metabolic Disorders

    MCAD deficiency

    TriggerFasting or intercurrent illness.
    PatternHypoketotic hypoglycemia with lethargy, vomiting, seizures/coma, and possible liver dysfunction.
    PreventionAvoid prolonged fasting and provide carbohydrate during illness.
    Board pearlHypoglycemia without an appropriate ketone response should trigger concern for a fatty-acid oxidation defect.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Metabolic Disorders

    Von Gierke disease (GSD I)

    DefectGlucose-6-phosphatase deficiency.
    PatternSevere fasting hypoglycemia with lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia, hyperlipidemia, and hepatomegaly.
    Management conceptFrequent carbohydrate delivery/avoid fasting; uncooked cornstarch is a classic long-term strategy.
    Board pearlHepatomegaly + fasting hypoglycemia + lactic acidosis is the classic GSD I pattern.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Peroxisomal, copper & purine disorders

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Metabolic Disorders

    Zellweger spectrum disorder

    MechanismPeroxisomal biogenesis disorder causing accumulation of very-long-chain fatty acids.
    Infant patternSevere hypotonia, poor feeding, seizures, craniofacial abnormalities, and hepatic/renal dysfunction.
    Other cluesNeuronal migration abnormalities and skeletal stippling may be present.
    Board pearl Severe neonatal hypotonia + liver disease + elevated very-long-chain fatty acids is a classic Zellweger pattern.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Metabolic Disorders

    Menkes disease

    MechanismX-linked ATP7A defect causing impaired copper transport.
    PatternNeurodegeneration beginning in infancy with sparse, brittle, lightly pigmented “kinky” hair.
    LabsLow copper and ceruloplasmin after the neonatal period.
    Board pearl Kinky brittle hair plus infantile neurodegeneration should trigger Menkes disease.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Metabolic Disorders

    Lesch-Nyhan syndrome

    MechanismHGPRT deficiency → impaired purine salvage and excess uric acid production.
    PatternDevelopmental/motor dysfunction, dystonia, and characteristic self-injurious behavior.
    OtherHyperuricemia can cause nephrolithiasis and gouty manifestations.
    Board pearl Self-mutilation + dystonia + hyperuricemia is the classic Lesch-Nyhan triad.

    Protein-energy malnutrition

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Nutrition

    Kwashiorkor vs marasmus

    KwashiorkorPredominant protein deficiency: edema, hypoalbuminemia, fatty liver, hair/skin changes, apathy and “flaky-paint” dermatitis.
    MarasmusSevere overall calorie deficiency: marked wasting and loss of subcutaneous fat without the prominent edema of kwashiorkor.
    Clinical riskBoth severe malnutrition states carry infection, electrolyte, and refeeding risks.
    Board pearlEdematous malnutrition = kwashiorkor; severe wasting without edema = marasmus.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Micronutrient deficiencies

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Nutrition

    Nutritional rickets

    MechanismVitamin D deficiency or inadequate calcium/phosphate mineralization.
    FindingsCraniotabes, widened wrists/ankles, rachitic rosary, bowed legs, delayed fontanel closure, and growth impairment.
    Labs patternTypically elevated alkaline phosphatase with secondary hyperparathyroidism; calcium may be low or normal depending on stage.
    Board pearlRickets is a mineralization disorder of growing bone; think wrists, ribs, legs, and growth plate abnormalities.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Nutrition

    Zinc deficiency / acrodermatitis enteropathica

    RashErosive or eczematous dermatitis around the mouth, anus, and distal extremities.
    Other cluesAlopecia, diarrhea, poor growth, impaired wound healing, and altered taste can occur.
    MechanismAcrodermatitis enteropathica is an inherited disorder of zinc absorption; acquired deficiency occurs with poor intake or malabsorption.
    Board pearl Periorificial + acral dermatitis with diarrhea/alopecia is a high-yield zinc-deficiency pattern.
    COMPARE / CONTRAST

    Vitamin deficiency pattern recognition

    Vitamin ANight blindness/xerophthalmia; severe deficiency can threaten the cornea.
    Thiamine (B1)Neuropathy/encephalopathy or high-output cardiac failure.
    Niacin (B3)Dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia.
    Vitamin CBleeding gums, bruising, bone pain, poor wound healing.
    Vitamin DRickets with metaphyseal cupping/fraying and widened growth plates.
    Vitamin ENeuropathy/ataxia and hemolysis, especially with fat malabsorption.
    Use the organ system pattern—eye, neuro, skin/GI, bone—to narrow the vitamin quickly.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Fluids & dehydration

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Nutrition

    Dehydration severity: use the exam

    MildOften subtle thirst and slightly decreased urine output.
    ModerateTachycardia, dry mucosa, decreased tears/urine, delayed capillary refill, and reduced skin turgor become more apparent.
    SeverePoor perfusion, lethargy, weak pulses, hypotension, and marked oliguria signal shock and require urgent resuscitation.
    Board pearl In children, perfusion and mental status are more useful than trying to infer dehydration from a single isolated sign.

    Allergy & Immunology

    Combined / T-cell immunodeficiency

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Allergy & Immunology

    Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID)

    RecognizeEarly severe/recurrent infections, chronic diarrhea, failure to thrive, opportunistic infections, and absent/small lymphoid tissue.
    Immune defectProfound T-cell dysfunction with secondary impairment of humoral immunity.
    SafetyAvoid live vaccines and nonirradiated blood products.
    TreatmentHematopoietic stem-cell transplantation is definitive for many forms.
    Board pearlInfant with thrush + chronic diarrhea + recurrent severe infections = SCID until proven otherwise.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Allergy & Immunology

    DiGeorge syndrome

    Cause22q11.2 deletion with abnormal pharyngeal pouch development.
    Classic patternConotruncal cardiac disease, abnormal facies/cleft palate, thymic hypoplasia, and hypocalcemia from hypoparathyroidism.
    Immune issueVariable T-cell deficiency; severe cases must avoid live vaccines.
    Board pearlConotruncal heart defect + hypocalcemia + recurrent infections = DiGeorge.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    B-cell / antibody deficiency

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Allergy & Immunology

    X-linked agammaglobulinemia

    DefectBTK mutation → failure of B-cell maturation.
    TimingRecurrent bacterial/enteroviral infections begin after maternal IgG wanes, typically later in infancy.
    ExamVery small/absent tonsils and lymph nodes.
    LabsMarkedly decreased B cells and immunoglobulins.
    Board pearlBoy with recurrent encapsulated bacterial infections after ~6 months + absent tonsils = XLA.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Allergy & Immunology

    Selective IgA deficiency

    PatternOften asymptomatic; some patients have recurrent sinopulmonary/GI infections, allergies, or autoimmune disease.
    Transfusion issueAnti-IgA antibodies can cause severe reactions to blood products in a subset of patients.
    AssociationCan coexist with celiac disease, but IgA-based celiac serologies may be falsely negative.
    Board pearl Low IgA can hide celiac disease on an IgA-based screen—check total IgA or use IgG-based testing when appropriate.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Phagocyte disorders

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Allergy & Immunology

    Chronic granulomatous disease

    DefectNADPH oxidase dysfunction → impaired respiratory burst.
    InfectionsRecurrent infections with catalase-positive organisms and granuloma formation.
    TestingAbnormal dihydrorhodamine flow cytometry/oxidative burst testing.
    Board pearlCatalase-positive infections + granulomas = CGD.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Allergy & Immunology

    Hyper-IgE syndrome

    PatternEczema, recurrent “cold” staphylococcal abscesses, and recurrent pneumonias.
    Other cluesVery high IgE, coarse facies, retained primary teeth, and skeletal abnormalities may occur.
    MechanismClassic autosomal dominant disease is associated with STAT3 dysfunction and impaired Th17 responses.
    Board pearl Cold abscesses + eczema + very high IgE is the board pattern for hyper-IgE syndrome.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Syndromic immunodeficiency

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Allergy & Immunology

    Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome

    TriadEczema, recurrent infections, and thrombocytopenia with small platelets.
    InheritanceX-linked.
    Long-termHigher risk of autoimmunity and lymphoid malignancy.
    Board pearlEczema + infections + small platelets is the classic WAS triad.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Complement deficiency

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Allergy & Immunology

    Terminal complement deficiency

    DefectC5–C9 deficiency impairs membrane attack complex formation.
    Infection patternRecurrent Neisseria infections are the classic clue.
    Board pearlRecurrent meningococcal disease should prompt evaluation of terminal complement function.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Bradykinin-mediated disease

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Allergy & Immunology

    Hereditary angioedema

    MechanismC1 esterase inhibitor deficiency/dysfunction → bradykinin-mediated angioedema.
    PatternRecurrent nonpruritic swelling of skin, GI tract, or airway without urticaria.
    Treatment clueEpinephrine/antihistamines are not reliably effective because this is not histamine-mediated; use targeted bradykinin/C1 inhibitor therapy for significant attacks.
    Board pearl Angioedema without hives—especially with abdominal attacks—should make you think bradykinin rather than allergy.

    Infectious Disease

    11 snapshots · 1 comparisons · 1080 unique facts
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Viral syndromes

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Infectious Disease

    Mumps

    PresentationParotid tenderness/swelling that may obscure the mandibular angle; Stensen duct can be erythematous/enlarged.
    IncubationTypically about 16–18 days, often with fever/malaise/anorexia before parotitis.
    ComplicationsEpididymo-orchitis is common in adolescent/postpubertal males; aseptic meningitis, pancreatitis, oophoritis and hearing loss can occur.
    DiagnosisUsually clinical; PCR from a buccal specimen is the preferred confirmatory approach when testing is needed.
    Board pearlParotitis + orchitis in an underimmunized adolescent is a classic mumps pattern.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Infectious Disease

    EBV infectious mononucleosis

    PatternFever, pharyngitis, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, fatigue, and splenomegaly.
    LabsAtypical lymphocytosis; heterophile testing is less reliable in young children.
    PearlA diffuse rash after amoxicillin/ampicillin in a patient with EBV is a classic association.
    Board pearl Posterior cervical nodes + pharyngitis + splenomegaly is the classic EBV triad.
    COMPARE / CONTRAST

    Viral exanthems: fastest discriminators

    MeaslesCough, coryza, conjunctivitis, Koplik spots → cephalocaudal rash.
    RubellaMilder illness, postauricular/posterior cervical nodes, fine rash.
    RoseolaHigh fever that resolves before the rash appears.
    Erythema infectiosum“Slapped-cheek” rash followed by lacy reticular eruption.
    VaricellaPruritic vesicles in multiple stages of evolution.
    The timing of fever relative to the rash is often the best separator.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Regional lymphadenitis & genital/perineal infection

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Infectious Disease

    Cat-scratch disease

    CauseBartonella henselae after cat exposure, especially scratches/bites.
    TypicalPapule at inoculation site followed by regional tender lymphadenitis.
    AtypicalParinaud oculoglandular syndrome: unilateral conjunctival inflammation/granuloma with ipsilateral preauricular nodes.
    TreatmentMost uncomplicated cases are self-limited; azithromycin can hasten lymph-node resolution. Aspirate suppurative nodes rather than routine incision/drainage.
    Board pearlRegional lymphadenitis after a cat scratch is usually enough to make the diagnosis clinically.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Infectious Disease

    GAS vulvovaginitis and perianal disease

    VulvovaginitisPrepubertal girl with sharply demarcated intense vulvar erythema, serous discharge, dysuria or movement discomfort, usually without systemic illness.
    Perianal diseaseBright/sharply bordered perianal erythema with painful defecation, pruritus, or blood-streaked stool.
    TreatmentAmoxicillin or a cephalosporin; reinforce gentle perineal hygiene for vulvovaginitis.
    Board pearlMarked, sharply demarcated erythema in a prepubertal child should make GAS part of the differential.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Infectious Disease

    Lymphogranuloma venereum

    CauseChlamydia trachomatis serovars L1–L3.
    CourseTransient painless/asymptomatic genital ulcer followed 2–6 weeks later by painful regional lymphadenopathy/buboes and constitutional symptoms.
    Groove signInguinal and femoral nodes enlarge above and below the inguinal ligament.
    TreatmentDoxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 21 days.
    Board pearlA healed painless ulcer followed weeks later by painful inguinal buboes is the classic LGV sequence.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Gastrointestinal infection

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Infectious Disease

    Bacterial gastroenteritis: pattern clues

    CampylobacterPoultry/contaminated water; febrile inflammatory diarrhea. Later Guillain-Barré syndrome or reactive arthritis can occur.
    ShigellaVery low infectious dose; inflammatory/bloody diarrhea, seizures in young children, and HUS risk with Shiga toxin-producing strains.
    Nontyphoidal SalmonellaEggs, poultry, reptiles; usually self-limited gastroenteritis but invasive disease risk rises in young infants and immunocompromised patients.
    Board pearlExposure history plus inflammatory versus watery diarrhea often narrows the bacterial differential quickly.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    CNS infection

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Infectious Disease

    Meningitis: age-based organism framework

    NeonatesGroup B Streptococcus, E coli and other gram-negative enteric bacilli, and Listeria are classic concerns.
    Older infants/childrenStreptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis dominate in appropriately immunized populations.
    Clinical ruleDo not delay empiric therapy in a toxic child when bacterial meningitis is strongly suspected.
    Board pearlAge and immunization status are central to choosing empiric meningitis coverage.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Congenital infection

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Infectious Disease

    Congenital infection: fast distinctions

    CMVPeriventricular calcifications, microcephaly, sensorineural hearing loss, petechiae/hepatosplenomegaly.
    ToxoplasmosisDiffuse intracranial calcifications, hydrocephalus, chorioretinitis.
    RubellaCataracts, PDA, hearing loss; “blueberry muffin” rash may occur.
    SyphilisSnuffles, rash involving palms/soles, hepatosplenomegaly, bone abnormalities; later Hutchinson teeth/saddle nose.
    Board pearlIntracranial calcification pattern is a classic CMV-versus-toxoplasmosis discriminator.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Respiratory infection

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Infectious Disease

    Pertussis

    StagesCatarrhal URI-like phase → paroxysmal coughing phase with whoop/posttussive emesis → gradual convalescence.
    InfantsYoung infants may present with apnea rather than a classic whoop.
    TreatmentMacrolide therapy reduces transmission; close contacts generally require postexposure management according to current guidance.
    Board pearl Apnea in a young infant with a household cough illness can be pertussis even without a whoop.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Vector-borne infection

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Infectious Disease

    Lyme disease

    EarlyErythema migrans is an expanding annular lesion and is a clinical diagnosis in the right exposure setting.
    DisseminatedFacial nerve palsy, meningitis, carditis, and migratory musculoskeletal symptoms can occur.
    LateLarge-joint arthritis—especially the knee—is a classic later manifestation.
    Board pearl Erythema migrans does not require serology before treatment when the presentation is classic.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Bone infection

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Infectious Disease

    Osteomyelitis: infectious pattern

    Most commonStaphylococcus aureus is the leading cause in otherwise healthy children.
    Special risksSalmonella is classically associated with sickle cell disease; puncture through a sneaker raises concern for Pseudomonas.
    DiagnosisMRI is highly sensitive when osteomyelitis is suspected and plain films are unrevealing early.
    Board pearl Bone pain + fever + focal tenderness should be treated as osteomyelitis until proven otherwise, especially when the child refuses to use the limb.

    SYSTEM

    Cardiology

    11 snapshots · 1 comparisons · 277 unique facts
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Left-to-right shunts

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Cardiology

    Ventricular septal defect

    MurmurHarsh holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border.
    Small VSDOften loud murmur but few symptoms.
    Large VSDPulmonary overcirculation → tachypnea, poor feeding, diaphoresis, failure to thrive, and heart failure after pulmonary vascular resistance falls.
    Board pearlA smaller VSD can sound louder than a large nonrestrictive defect.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Cardiology

    Atrial septal defect

    ExamFixed, widely split S2 with a systolic ejection murmur from increased flow across the pulmonic valve.
    CourseOften asymptomatic in childhood; large defects cause right-sided volume overload over time.
    Board pearlFixed split S2 is the board-defining ASD finding.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Cardiology

    Patent ductus arteriosus

    MurmurContinuous “machine-like” murmur, classically at the left infraclavicular/upper sternal border.
    PulseBounding pulses and widened pulse pressure may occur with a significant shunt.
    PrematurityHemodynamically significant PDA is particularly common in premature infants.
    Board pearlContinuous murmur + bounding pulses = PDA.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Cyanotic congenital heart disease

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Cardiology

    Tetralogy of Fallot and tet spells

    AnatomyVSD, overriding aorta, right ventricular outflow obstruction/pulmonary stenosis, and RV hypertrophy.
    Tet spellAbrupt increase in right-to-left shunting causes profound cyanosis, often with crying/feeding.
    Immediate maneuversKnee-chest position, oxygen and calming; additional pharmacologic management reduces infundibular spasm and improves systemic vascular resistance.
    Board pearlSquatting/knee-chest raises systemic vascular resistance and reduces right-to-left shunting.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Cardiology

    Transposition of the great arteries

    PhysiologyParallel systemic and pulmonary circulations; survival depends on mixing through an ASD/VSD/PDA.
    PresentationProfound cyanosis early in life, often with relatively little respiratory distress.
    StabilizeProstaglandin E1 maintains ductal patency while definitive intervention is arranged; atrial septostomy may be needed to improve mixing.
    Board pearl Severe neonatal cyanosis with little improvement on oxygen should raise concern for TGA and another ductal/mixing-dependent lesion.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Cardiology

    Truncus arteriosus

    AnatomySingle arterial trunk supplies systemic, pulmonary, and coronary circulations and is associated with a VSD.
    PatternEarly cyanosis plus heart failure as pulmonary blood flow increases.
    AssociationConotruncal defects are associated with 22q11.2 deletion/DiGeorge syndrome.
    Board pearl A single outflow tract + VSD is truncus arteriosus; think 22q11.2 deletion.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Cardiology

    Total anomalous pulmonary venous return

    AnatomyPulmonary veins return to the systemic venous circulation rather than the left atrium; an interatrial communication is required.
    Obstructed formCan cause severe neonatal cyanosis, respiratory distress, and pulmonary edema.
    Unobstructed formMay present with milder cyanosis and right-sided volume overload.
    Board pearl Obstructed TAPVR is a neonatal emergency and can look like severe lung disease with cyanosis.
    COMPARE / CONTRAST

    Cyanotic congenital heart disease: quick physiology map

    TOFDecreased pulmonary blood flow; tet spells; improves with knee-chest position.
    TGAParallel circulations; needs mixing; profound early cyanosis.
    Truncus arteriosusSingle outflow trunk + VSD; cyanosis and early heart failure.
    TAPVRPulmonary veins drain systemically; obstructed form causes severe cyanosis/pulmonary edema.
    In a critically cyanotic neonate, ask whether survival depends on ductal patency or mixing.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Obstructive congenital lesion

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Cardiology

    Coarctation of the aorta

    ExamUpper-extremity hypertension with weak/delayed femoral pulses and lower-extremity pressure.
    InfantsCritical coarctation may present with shock when the ductus closes.
    AssociationsTurner syndrome and bicuspid aortic valve.
    Board pearlAlways palpate femoral pulses in an infant or child with hypertension or unexplained shock.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Acquired & inflammatory heart disease

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Cardiology

    Kawasaki disease

    RecognizeProlonged fever plus mucocutaneous inflammation: conjunctivitis, oral changes, rash, extremity changes, and cervical lymphadenopathy.
    Major riskCoronary artery aneurysms and thrombosis.
    TreatmentIVIG plus aspirin; obtain echocardiographic surveillance.
    Board pearlThe reason to diagnose Kawasaki promptly is coronary protection.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Cardiology

    Myocarditis in children

    PresentationTachycardia out of proportion to fever, exercise intolerance, respiratory/GI symptoms, chest pain, syncope, or new heart failure.
    CluesCardiomegaly, ventricular dysfunction, arrhythmia, and elevated cardiac biomarkers may occur.
    PearlInfants can present nonspecifically with poor feeding, diaphoresis, and respiratory distress.
    Board pearl Unexplained persistent tachycardia plus heart-failure findings after a viral illness should raise concern for myocarditis.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Murmur evaluation

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Cardiology

    Innocent vs pathologic murmur

    Innocent cluesSoft, systolic, position-dependent, normal S2, no click, normal pulses, and an otherwise well child.
    Pathologic cluesDiastolic or holosystolic murmur, harsh quality, click, abnormal S2, thrill, cyanosis, poor growth, syncope/chest pain with exertion, or abnormal pulses.
    Board pearlA diastolic murmur is pathologic until proven otherwise.

    Pulmonology

    7 snapshots · 2 comparisons · 131 unique facts
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Asthma & recurrent wheeze

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Pulmonology

    Asthma exacerbation: acute priorities

    First-lineInhaled short-acting beta agonist; add ipratropium for moderate/severe exacerbations and systemic corticosteroid early when indicated.
    Severity cluesSpeech limitation, retractions, poor air movement, hypoxemia, altered mental status, or a “silent chest” indicate severe disease.
    DangerA normalizing or rising PaCO2 in a tiring patient is ominous because early asthma typically causes hypocapnia.
    Board pearlThe quiet chest in a distressed asthmatic is worse than loud wheezing.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Pulmonology

    Asthma Predictive Index

    UseYoung children (≤3 years) with recurrent wheezing; estimates risk of persistent asthma.
    High riskAt least 1 major criterion or at least 2 minor criteria.
    MajorParental physician-diagnosed asthma or atopic dermatitis in the child.
    MinorAllergic rhinitis, wheezing apart from colds/URIs, or peripheral eosinophilia.
    Board pearlParental asthma is one of the strongest recurrent-wheeze predictors in toddlers.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Chronic / multisystem disease

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Pulmonology

    Cystic fibrosis

    PulmonaryChronic/recurrent sinopulmonary infection, bronchiectasis, and progressive obstructive lung disease.
    GIPancreatic insufficiency → steatorrhea, poor growth, and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency; meconium ileus can be the neonatal clue.
    DiagnosisNewborn screening followed by confirmatory sweat chloride and/or CFTR testing.
    Board pearlMeconium ileus or recurrent sinopulmonary disease plus poor growth should trigger CF evaluation.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Pulmonology

    Obstructive sleep apnea in children

    Common causeAdenotonsillar hypertrophy is a major cause in otherwise healthy children; obesity increases risk.
    CluesSnoring, witnessed apneas, restless sleep, enuresis, morning headaches, behavioral/attention problems, or poor school performance.
    DiagnosisPolysomnography is the definitive diagnostic test when needed.
    Board pearl Pediatric OSA may present as hyperactivity or school problems rather than daytime sleepiness.
    COMPARE / CONTRAST

    Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency: CF vs Shwachman-Diamond

    FeatureCystic fibrosisShwachman-Diamond syndrome
    Sweat chlorideElevated / diagnostic when criteria are metNormal
    HematologyNo characteristic cyclic neutropeniaChronic, intermittent, or cyclic neutropenia; anemia/thrombocytopenia may coexist
    InfectionsPredominantly sinopulmonary from impaired mucociliary clearanceBacterial/fungal risk from neutropenia plus neutrophil dysfunction
    Skeletal cluesNot a defining featureMetaphyseal/growth-plate abnormalities, thoracic/digital abnormalities
    Pancreatic courseExocrine insufficiency is typically persistentExocrine function may improve with age; a substantial subset normalizes by early childhood
    Pancreatic treatmentPancreatic enzymes + fat-soluble vitamins when insufficientPancreatic enzymes + fat-soluble vitamins while insufficiency persists
    Board discriminator: steatorrhea/growth faltering + normal sweat chloride + neutropenia strongly favors Shwachman-Diamond over cystic fibrosis.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Lower respiratory infection

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Pulmonology

    Bronchiolitis

    WhoUsually infants/toddlers with a viral prodrome followed by cough, tachypnea, wheeze/crackles, and increased work of breathing.
    TreatmentSupportive care: nasal suctioning, hydration, and oxygen when indicated.
    Avoid routinelyBronchodilators, corticosteroids, antibiotics, and chest radiographs are not routine therapy for uncomplicated bronchiolitis.
    Board pearl A first episode of wheezing in an infant during a viral illness is usually bronchiolitis, and treatment is supportive.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Pulmonology

    Pediatric pneumonia: pattern clues

    Typical bacterialAbrupt fever, focal findings, and lobar consolidation suggest pneumococcal-type bacterial pneumonia.
    AtypicalSchool-age child/adolescent with gradual cough, headache, malaise, and diffuse findings suggests Mycoplasma.
    ComplicationPersistent fever, respiratory distress, or focal dullness/decreased breath sounds should raise concern for parapneumonic effusion/empyema.
    Board pearl Age and tempo matter: focal abrupt disease points bacterial; gradual diffuse disease in an older child points atypical.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Upper airway & aspiration

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Pulmonology

    Foreign-body aspiration

    Classic eventSudden choking/coughing episode in a toddler followed by persistent cough, unilateral wheeze, or asymmetric breath sounds.
    ImagingCan be normal; expiratory/decubitus films may show unilateral air trapping.
    DefinitiveRigid bronchoscopy when suspicion is high.
    Board pearlA normal chest radiograph does not exclude an aspirated foreign body.
    COMPARE / CONTRAST

    Upper-airway emergencies: croup vs epiglottitis vs bacterial tracheitis

    CroupBarking cough, hoarseness, inspiratory stridor; usually viral and gradual. Treat with dexamethasone; add nebulized epinephrine for moderate/severe disease.
    EpiglottitisToxic appearance, high fever, drooling, dysphagia, tripod posture. Avoid agitation and secure the airway in a controlled setting before routine throat examination.
    Bacterial tracheitisToxic child with high fever/stridor and thick secretions, often after a viral prodrome; poor response to usual croup therapy and may require airway support plus IV antibiotics.
    Drooling/toxic appearance is not typical simple croup.

    SYSTEM

    Gastroenterology

    12 snapshots · 1 comparisons · 212 unique facts
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Infant vomiting & obstruction

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Gastroenterology

    Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis

    PresentationYoung infant with progressive nonbilious projectile vomiting, persistent hunger, and possible dehydration/weight loss.
    ExamPalpable epigastric “olive” and visible gastric peristalsis may occur.
    LabsHypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis in more advanced cases.
    DiagnosisUltrasound; supportive thresholds include pyloric muscle thickness >3 mm or canal length >18 mm.
    TreatmentCorrect fluids/electrolytes first, then pyloromyotomy.
    Board pearlPyloric stenosis is a medical resuscitation problem before it is a surgical problem.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Gastroenterology

    Malrotation with midgut volvulus

    PresentationBilious vomiting in a neonate/young infant is the classic emergency presentation.
    Why dangerousVolvulus can rapidly compromise mesenteric blood flow and cause bowel necrosis.
    ActionUrgent surgical evaluation; upper GI contrast study is the classic diagnostic study in a stable patient.
    Board pearlBilious vomiting in an infant is intestinal obstruction until proven otherwise.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Gastroenterology

    Intussusception

    AgeMost common in infants/toddlers, especially about 6–36 months.
    PresentationIntermittent severe colicky pain, vomiting, lethargy; currant-jelly stool is a late finding.
    ImagingUltrasound target/doughnut sign.
    TreatmentAir or contrast enema is diagnostic and therapeutic when there is no perforation/peritonitis.
    Board pearlEpisodic pain + lethargy in a toddler can be intussusception even before bloody stool appears.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Gastroenterology

    Hirschsprung disease

    CluesFailure to pass meconium in the first 48 hours, abdominal distention, bilious vomiting, and explosive stool after rectal exam.
    MechanismAganglionosis from failed neural-crest migration causes a tonically contracted distal segment with proximal dilation.
    DiagnosisRectal suction biopsy demonstrating absent ganglion cells.
    Board pearlDelayed meconium + explosive stool after rectal exam = Hirschsprung.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Gastroenterology

    Gastroesophageal reflux vs GERD in infancy

    Physiologic refluxEffortless spit-ups in a thriving, comfortable infant are common and usually resolve with maturation.
    GERDPoor weight gain, feeding refusal, hematemesis, significant respiratory complications, or persistent pain suggest disease rather than physiologic reflux.
    PearlAcid-suppressive medication is not indicated for uncomplicated “happy spitting.”
    Board pearl The thriving “happy spitter” needs reassurance and feeding guidance, not routine acid suppression.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Abdominal pain & surgical disease

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Gastroenterology

    Appendicitis in children

    EvolutionPeriumbilical pain migrates to the right lower quadrant as parietal peritoneum becomes inflamed.
    AssociatedAnorexia, nausea/vomiting and fever are common; younger children may present atypically.
    ImagingUltrasound is generally the first imaging study in children when imaging is needed.
    Board pearlPain usually precedes vomiting in appendicitis; vomiting preceding pain suggests another diagnosis.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Gastroenterology

    Meckel diverticulum

    PatternPainless lower GI bleeding in a child is the classic presentation; diverticulitis or obstruction can mimic appendicitis.
    MechanismEctopic gastric mucosa can ulcerate adjacent ileal mucosa.
    DiagnosisTechnetium-99m pertechnetate scan identifies ectopic gastric mucosa.
    Board pearl Painless maroon/bright-red rectal bleeding in a child should put Meckel diverticulum near the top of the list.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Gastroenterology

    Functional constipation

    PatternPainful/hard stools, stool withholding, large-caliber stools, and fecal soiling in an otherwise thriving child.
    Red flagsDelayed meconium, failure to thrive, severe abdominal distention, neurologic findings, blood without fissure, or abnormal anal/spine exam suggest an organic cause.
    TreatmentDisimpaction when needed, then maintenance osmotic laxative therapy plus scheduled toilet sitting and behavioral support.
    Board pearl Most childhood constipation is functional; red flags—not duration alone—drive the search for Hirschsprung disease or another organic cause.
    COMPARE / CONTRAST

    GI bleeding in children: high-yield localization

    Painless lower GI bleedingMeckel diverticulum is a classic board answer.
    Pain + currant-jelly stoolIntussusception.
    Bloody diarrhea after infectious prodromeConsider bacterial enteritis; HUS risk depends on pathogen/toxin.
    Anal pain + streaks of bright bloodAnal fissure, often from constipation.
    Painful vs painless bleeding is a useful first split.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Malabsorption & intestinal inflammation

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Gastroenterology

    Celiac disease

    PresentationChronic diarrhea, abdominal distention, poor growth, iron deficiency, or extraintestinal manifestations.
    ScreeningTissue transglutaminase IgA with total IgA level is the usual initial serology.
    DiagnosisSmall-bowel biopsy shows villous atrophy when confirmation is required.
    TreatmentStrict lifelong gluten-free diet.
    Board pearlUnexplained iron deficiency or poor growth can be the presenting clue to celiac disease.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Gastroenterology

    IBD: Crohn vs ulcerative colitis

    CrohnTransmural, skip lesions anywhere mouth-to-anus; fistulas, strictures, perianal disease and growth failure are classic.
    UCContinuous mucosal inflammation beginning in the rectum and limited to the colon; bloody diarrhea is common.
    SharedExtraintestinal arthritis, eye disease, skin disease, and hepatobiliary complications can occur.
    Board pearlPerianal disease/skip lesions favor Crohn; continuous rectal disease favors UC.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Pancreatic disease

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Gastroenterology

    Hereditary pancreatitis genetics

    PRSS1Most common classic hereditary cause; usually autosomal dominant. Encodes cationic trypsinogen.
    MechanismPathogenic variants promote premature intrapancreatic trypsin activity and autodigestion; R122H and N29I are classic variants.
    SPINK1Encodes a pancreatic trypsin inhibitor; variants usually act as susceptibility/disease-modifying alleles rather than a highly penetrant monogenic cause.
    Board pearlRecurrent pancreatitis across generations strongly suggests PRSS1-associated hereditary pancreatitis.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Gastroenterology

    Acute pancreatitis in children

    DiagnosisRequires compatible abdominal pain, elevated pancreatic enzymes, and/or characteristic imaging—typically two of three criteria.
    Common causesMedications, systemic illness/trauma, biliary disease, infection, and genetic susceptibility are important pediatric causes.
    Initial careEarly enteral nutrition when tolerated, analgesia, and appropriate fluid/electrolyte support; investigate recurrent episodes for genetic/anatomic causes.
    Board pearl Recurrent pancreatitis in a child deserves evaluation for genetic susceptibility such as PRSS1 and SPINK1.

    SYSTEM

    Nephrology & Urology

    9 snapshots · 1 comparisons · 419 unique facts
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Glomerular & microangiopathic disease

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Nephrology & Urology

    Minimal-change nephrotic syndrome

    PatternHeavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, edema and hyperlipidemia.
    ChildrenMinimal-change disease is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children.
    TreatmentMost children respond to corticosteroids.
    ComplicationsInfection and thrombosis risk rise because immunoglobulins and anticoagulant proteins are lost in urine.
    Board pearlEdematous child with massive proteinuria and normal complement is classic minimal-change nephrotic syndrome.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Nephrology & Urology

    Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis

    TimingNephritic syndrome after recent group A streptococcal pharyngitis or skin infection.
    FindingsHematuria/cola urine, RBC casts, edema, hypertension and variable renal dysfunction.
    ComplementC3 is typically low and should recover with time.
    Board pearlNephritic syndrome + low C3 after strep infection = PSGN.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Nephrology & Urology

    Hemolytic uremic syndrome

    TriadMicroangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury.
    Typical triggerShiga toxin-producing diarrheal illness, classically bloody diarrhea.
    ManagementSupportive care is central in typical STEC-HUS; monitor renal function, volume, blood pressure and anemia.
    Board pearlBloody diarrhea followed by pallor, low platelets and AKI = HUS.
    COMPARE / CONTRAST

    Hematuria after infection: IgA vs PSGN

    IgA nephropathyHematuria during/within days of URI; complement usually normal.
    PSGNHematuria weeks after strep infection; low C3 and nephritic syndrome are typical.
    Synpharyngitic = IgA; delayed after strep = PSGN.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    UTI, reflux & obstructive uropathy

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Nephrology & Urology

    Pediatric UTI and vesicoureteral reflux

    InfantsUTI may present only with fever, vomiting, poor feeding, or irritability.
    DiagnosisObtain a properly collected urine sample for urinalysis and culture before antibiotics when feasible.
    VURRetrograde urine flow increases recurrent pyelonephritis/scarring risk; management depends on grade, recurrence and renal findings.
    Board pearlA febrile infant without a source needs UTI in the differential.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Nephrology & Urology

    Prune belly syndrome

    TriadDeficient abdominal musculature, urinary tract dilation/abnormalities, and cryptorchidism; predominantly affects males.
    ComplicationsRenal dysplasia, reflux/obstruction, recurrent UTI, progressive CKD and pulmonary hypoplasia from oligohydramnios.
    ManagementClose UTI surveillance; antimicrobial prophylaxis when obstruction is present; surgery may be needed for significant obstructive hydronephrosis.
    Board pearlThe pulmonary complication can be the immediately life-threatening part of severe prune belly syndrome.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Nephrology & Urology

    Posterior urethral valves

    WhoMale infant with bladder outlet obstruction.
    Prenatal/neonatal cluesBilateral hydronephrosis, enlarged thick-walled bladder, oligohydramnios, poor urinary stream, or renal dysfunction.
    ComplicationSevere fetal obstruction can cause pulmonary hypoplasia and chronic kidney disease.
    Board pearl Bilateral hydronephrosis + distended bladder in a male fetus/newborn should trigger posterior urethral valves.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Male genitourinary

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Nephrology & Urology

    Varicocele

    Exam“Bag of worms” dilated pampiniform plexus, usually left-sided and more prominent standing/Valsalva.
    FertilityRaised scrotal temperature may reduce sperm count/motility.
    Red flagsRight-sided varicocele or one that does not decompress supine suggests secondary venous obstruction and warrants abdominal evaluation.
    PreadolescentEvaluate for secondary abdominal/retroperitoneal pathology.
    Board pearlA new right-sided or nondecompressing varicocele is not a routine adolescent varicocele.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Voiding disorders

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Nephrology & Urology

    Primary monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis

    DefinitionNighttime bedwetting in a child old enough for expected nighttime continence, without daytime lower urinary tract symptoms.
    First stepsHistory, exam, urinalysis when indicated, constipation/sleep screening, and behavioral measures such as timed voiding and fluid management.
    TreatmentEnuresis alarm provides durable benefit; desmopressin is useful for rapid/temporary control in selected patients.
    Board pearl Daytime symptoms, recurrent UTIs, abnormal stream, neurologic signs, or secondary enuresis broaden the workup.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Nephrolithiasis

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Nephrology & Urology

    Pediatric nephrolithiasis

    PresentationFlank/abdominal pain, hematuria, dysuria, or recurrent UTI; younger children may present nonspecifically.
    EvaluationUrinalysis, imaging with ultrasound as a radiation-sparing first test in many children, and metabolic evaluation for recurrent/high-risk stones.
    RiskLow fluid intake, hypercalciuria, metabolic disease, infection, and selected medications can contribute.
    Board pearl Children with stones deserve more attention to metabolic causes than the typical adult with a first uncomplicated stone.

    Endocrinology

    9 snapshots · 0 comparisons · 395 unique facts
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Diabetes & glucose emergencies

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Endocrinology

    Type 1 diabetes mellitus: presentation

    ClassicPolyuria, polydipsia, nocturia/enuresis, weight loss, fatigue, and sometimes candidiasis.
    DKA clueVomiting, abdominal pain, dehydration, Kussmaul respirations, and altered mental status indicate diabetic ketoacidosis.
    Autoimmune contextThyroid and celiac autoimmunity are important associated conditions.
    Board pearl New bedwetting plus weight loss and polydipsia is a classic pediatric type 1 diabetes stem.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Endocrinology

    Diabetic ketoacidosis

    PatternHyperglycemia, ketosis and anion-gap metabolic acidosis with dehydration.
    SequenceBegin isotonic fluid resuscitation, then continuous insulin; add dextrose as glucose falls while continuing insulin until ketoacidosis resolves.
    PotassiumTotal body potassium is depleted even when initial serum potassium is normal/high.
    Major pediatric dangerCerebral injury/edema—watch for headache, altered mental status, bradycardia, vomiting or neurologic decline.
    Board pearlIn pediatric DKA, treat the ketoacidosis—not just the glucose—and watch closely for cerebral injury.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Thyroid disease

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Endocrinology

    Congenital hypothyroidism

    EarlyOften subtle because maternal thyroid hormone provides partial protection.
    CluesProlonged jaundice, large fontanel, macroglossia, hypotonia, constipation, poor feeding, umbilical hernia and hoarse cry.
    Why screening mattersUntreated disease can cause irreversible neurodevelopmental impairment.
    Board pearlNewborn screening allows treatment before the classic phenotype becomes obvious.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Endocrinology

    Graves disease in children

    PatternWeight loss despite appetite, heat intolerance, tremor, tachycardia, goiter, anxiety, and accelerated growth/bone age.
    LabsSuppressed TSH with elevated free T4/T3; TSH-receptor antibodies support Graves disease.
    EyeOphthalmopathy supports Graves but is not required.
    Board pearl Hyperthyroidism plus diffuse goiter in an adolescent is Graves disease until proven otherwise.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Adrenal disorders

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Endocrinology

    21-hydroxylase congenital adrenal hyperplasia

    HormonesLow cortisol ± low aldosterone with increased androgen production and elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone.
    GirlsVirilized/ambiguous external genitalia can be present at birth.
    Salt-wasting formVomiting, dehydration, hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia and hypoglycemia in early infancy.
    Board pearlA sick neonate with hyperkalemia + hyponatremia + ambiguous genitalia strongly suggests salt-wasting CAH.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Endocrinology

    Adrenal insufficiency

    PrimaryLow cortisol with high ACTH; may cause hyperpigmentation, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and volume depletion.
    CentralLow cortisol with low/inappropriately normal ACTH; hyperkalemia is less typical because aldosterone is preserved.
    CrisisShock, vomiting, abdominal pain, hypoglycemia, and electrolyte abnormalities require urgent stress-dose glucocorticoids and fluids.
    Board pearl Hyperpigmentation + hyperkalemia points to primary adrenal failure rather than central adrenal insufficiency.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Puberty & growth

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Endocrinology

    Precocious puberty: central vs peripheral

    CentralEarly activation of hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis; puberty occurs in normal sequence. GnRH stimulation produces a pubertal LH response.
    PeripheralSex-steroid exposure independent of central activation; consider adrenal/gonadal disorders, tumors or exogenous hormones.
    Bone ageUsually advanced when sex-steroid exposure is significant.
    Board pearlIs the HPG axis activated? That is the core central-versus-peripheral question.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Endocrinology

    Growth hormone deficiency

    GrowthPoor linear growth with preserved/increased weight for height.
    Bone ageDelayed.
    Other cluesNeonatal hypoglycemia, prolonged jaundice, or micropenis can suggest congenital pituitary dysfunction.
    Board pearl Endocrine short stature tends to preserve weight while height velocity falls.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Water balance

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Endocrinology

    Diabetes insipidus vs SIADH

    DILarge-volume dilute urine with hypernatremia/high serum osmolality if water intake is inadequate.
    SIADHHyponatremia with inappropriately concentrated urine and clinical euvolemia.
    Key dataCompare serum sodium/osmolality with urine osmolality and urine output.
    Board pearlDI cannot concentrate urine; SIADH cannot appropriately dilute it.
