    Hematology & Oncology

    11 snapshots · 1 comparisons · 446 unique facts
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Red-cell disorders

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Hematology & Oncology

    Iron deficiency vs thalassemia trait

    Iron deficiencyLow ferritin, increased RDW, low transferrin saturation; dietary risk or blood loss common.
    Thalassemia traitMicrocytosis is often disproportionate to the anemia, RDW may be normal, and RBC count is relatively preserved/high.
    SmearTarget cells favor thalassemia; marked anisopoikilocytosis is common in iron deficiency.
    Board pearlVery low MCV with a relatively high RBC count should make you think thalassemia trait.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Hematology & Oncology

    Sickle cell disease: pediatric priorities

    Early preventionPenicillin prophylaxis in young children and complete vaccination against encapsulated organisms.
    Acute chest syndromeNew pulmonary infiltrate plus respiratory symptoms/fever; treat aggressively with oxygen/support, antibiotics, pain control and transfusion when indicated.
    Splenic sequestrationAcute splenic enlargement with rapid anemia and hypovolemia in young children.
    Stroke riskTranscranial Doppler screening identifies high-risk children for preventive transfusion programs.
    Board pearlA falling hemoglobin with sudden splenomegaly in a young child with sickle cell disease is splenic sequestration until proven otherwise.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Hematology & Oncology

    G6PD deficiency

    PatternEpisodic hemolysis after oxidant stress such as infection, selected drugs, or fava beans.
    SmearBite cells and Heinz bodies are classic clues.
    Testing pearlEnzyme testing during/just after acute hemolysis can be falsely normal because young reticulocytes have higher G6PD activity.
    Board pearl Oxidant trigger + sudden hemolysis + bite cells = G6PD deficiency.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Hematology & Oncology

    Hereditary spherocytosis

    PatternCoombs-negative hemolytic anemia with jaundice, splenomegaly, reticulocytosis, and spherocytes.
    ComplicationsPigment gallstones and transient aplastic crisis with parvovirus B19.
    TestingEosin-5-maleimide binding or osmotic-fragility-type testing supports the diagnosis.
    Board pearl Spherocytes + negative direct antiglobulin test should make you think hereditary spherocytosis.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Platelets & coagulation

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Hematology & Oncology

    Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP)

    PatternIsolated thrombocytopenia in an otherwise well child, often after a viral infection; platelets are typically large.
    BleedingPetechiae, purpura and mucosal bleeding; hepatosplenomegaly or other cytopenias should prompt another diagnosis.
    TreatmentObservation is appropriate for many children with minor bleeding; IVIG or corticosteroids are used for more significant bleeding/selected severe thrombocytopenia.
    Board pearlIsolated low platelets in a well child after a viral illness is classic ITP.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Hematology & Oncology

    Hemophilia vs von Willebrand disease

    HemophiliaDeep tissue/joint bleeding, prolonged aPTT, normal platelet count; factor VIII (A) or IX (B) deficiency.
    vWDMucocutaneous bleeding, epistaxis/menorrhagia; platelet adhesion defect with variable aPTT elevation from reduced factor VIII stability.
    Board pearlHemarthroses favor hemophilia; mucosal bleeding favors vWD/platelet dysfunction.
    COMPARE / CONTRAST

    Bleeding pattern + labs

    ITPIsolated thrombocytopenia; mucocutaneous bleeding/petechiae.
    HemophiliaDeep tissue/joint bleeding; prolonged aPTT with normal PT/platelets.
    von Willebrand diseaseMucosal bleeding; platelet count usually normal; aPTT may be normal or mildly prolonged.
    DICThrombocytopenia + prolonged PT/aPTT + low fibrinogen + elevated fibrin degradation products.
    Mucosal = platelet/vWF problem; joints/deep tissue = coagulation-factor problem.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Leukemia & lymphoma

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Hematology & Oncology

    Acute leukemia in a child

    PresentationFatigue/pallor, fever/infections, bruising/bleeding, bone pain, lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly.
    CBCAnemia and thrombocytopenia are common; WBC can be low, normal or high.
    ALLMost common childhood leukemia; mediastinal mass suggests T-cell ALL.
    Board pearlDo not rule out leukemia because the total WBC count is normal.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Hematology & Oncology

    Burkitt lymphoma: pediatric pattern

    PresentationU.S. pediatric cases commonly involve the abdomen/ileocecal region and may present with an abdominal mass, pain, nausea/vomiting or intussusception.
    BiologyExtremely rapid proliferation; doubling time can be only 2–3 days.
    Immediate riskTumor lysis syndrome is common because of rapid growth and treatment response.
    Risk contextPediatric NHL risk rises with immunodeficiency/immunosuppression, including Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, ataxia-telangiectasia and HIV.
    Board pearlRapidly enlarging abdominal tumor in a child + tumor lysis risk → think Burkitt.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Hematology & Oncology

    Hodgkin lymphoma in adolescents

    PatternPainless cervical/supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, mediastinal mass, and possible B symptoms.
    ClueNodes are typically firm/rubbery and persistent rather than acutely tender.
    DiagnosisExcisional lymph-node biopsy is preferred when lymphoma is suspected.
    Board pearl Persistent painless supraclavicular/cervical adenopathy in an adolescent deserves a lymphoma workup.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Solid tumors

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Hematology & Oncology

    Wilms tumor vs neuroblastoma

    WilmsUsually a smooth unilateral renal mass, often does not cross midline; hematuria or hypertension may occur.
    NeuroblastomaAdrenal/sympathetic origin, often irregular and crosses midline; systemic symptoms, bone pain, periorbital ecchymoses, or opsoclonus-myoclonus may occur.
    MarkersUrinary catecholamine metabolites support neuroblastoma.
    Board pearlAbdominal mass crossing midline + catecholamine metabolites = neuroblastoma.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Oncologic emergencies

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Hematology & Oncology

    Tumor lysis syndrome

    LabsHyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, and hyperuricemia after rapid tumor-cell breakdown.
    High riskBurkitt lymphoma and other bulky, highly proliferative hematologic malignancies are classic high-risk settings.
    Prevention/treatmentAggressive hydration plus uric-acid–lowering therapy and close electrolyte/renal monitoring; rasburicase is used in high-risk or established hyperuricemia settings.
    Board pearl Burkitt lymphoma can lyse before or immediately after therapy—anticipate TLS rather than waiting for it.

    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Seizures

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Neurology

    Simple vs complex febrile seizure

    SimpleGeneralized, <15 minutes, and occurs once in 24 hours in a neurologically healthy child with fever.
    ComplexFocal, ≥15 minutes, or recurrent within 24 hours.
    TestingRoutine neuroimaging/EEG is not needed for a typical simple febrile seizure; evaluate for meningitis when clinical features warrant.
    Board pearlThe seizure classification drives the workup more than the height of the fever.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Neurology

    Infantile spasms

    RecognizeClusters of brief flexor/extensor spasms in infancy, often on awakening, with developmental arrest/regression.
    EEGHypsarrhythmia.
    TreatmentACTH or high-dose corticosteroid is classic first-line therapy; vigabatrin is particularly important with tuberous sclerosis.
    Board pearlInfant with developmental regression + clusters of spasms + hypsarrhythmia = infantile spasms.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Neurology

    Absence seizures

    PresentationBrief staring spells with abrupt onset/offset, no postictal confusion, often many times daily.
    EEGGeneralized 3-Hz spike-and-wave.
    ProvocationHyperventilation can trigger an event during examination/EEG.
    TreatmentEthosuximide is classic first-line for isolated absence seizures.
    Board pearlSeconds-long staring with immediate return to baseline is different from focal impaired-awareness seizure.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Neurology

    Status epilepticus: initial sequence

    FirstStabilize airway/breathing/circulation and check glucose while treating an ongoing convulsive seizure promptly.
    MedicationA benzodiazepine is first-line acute antiseizure therapy; persistent seizures require a second-line antiseizure medication.
    CauseConsider fever/infection, electrolyte or glucose abnormalities, toxic ingestion, trauma, medication nonadherence, and structural disease.
    Board pearl Do not delay benzodiazepine treatment of an ongoing convulsive seizure while waiting for diagnostic testing.
    COMPARE / CONTRAST

    Common pediatric seizure patterns

    AbsenceBrief staring with abrupt start/stop, no postictal state; generalized 3-Hz spike-wave.
    Infantile spasmsClusters of flexor/extensor spasms in infancy with developmental regression; hypsarrhythmia.
    Febrile seizureAge-appropriate child with fever and no CNS infection/metabolic cause; classify simple vs complex by duration, focality, and recurrence.
    Focal seizureFocal motor/sensory/autonomic onset; may impair awareness or generalize.
    Age + duration + postictal state are powerful seizure discriminators.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Headache

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Neurology

    Headache red flags in children

    ConcerningFocal neurologic deficit, papilledema, altered mental status, seizures, morning/positional vomiting, rapidly progressive pattern, systemic illness, or very young age with new severe headache.
    PrincipleNeuroimaging is driven by red flags and abnormal examination, not by uncomplicated recurrent migraine alone.
    Board pearlA normal neurologic examination and a stable recurrent migraine pattern are reassuring; papilledema changes the game.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Neurology

    Migraine in children

    PatternRecurrent episodic headache with nausea/vomiting and/or photophobia/phonophobia; pain may be bilateral in younger children.
    AuraTransient focal neurologic symptoms can precede headache in migraine with aura.
    Red flagsAbnormal neurologic exam, progressive pattern, persistent early-morning vomiting, seizures, or signs of raised intracranial pressure require evaluation for secondary causes.
    Board pearl A normal neurologic exam and stereotyped recurrent episodes strongly support primary migraine.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Neuromuscular disease

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Neurology

    Duchenne muscular dystrophy

    PatternBoy with proximal weakness, delayed motor milestones, Gowers sign, calf pseudohypertrophy, and markedly elevated CK.
    GeneticsX-linked dystrophin mutation, often frameshift/out-of-frame in Duchenne.
    ComplicationsProgressive cardiomyopathy and respiratory muscle weakness require surveillance.
    Board pearl Gowers sign + calf pseudohypertrophy + very high CK in a boy = Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

    Rheumatology

    7 snapshots · 0 comparisons · 120 unique facts
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Arthritis & postinfectious inflammation

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Rheumatology

    Juvenile idiopathic arthritis

    DefinitionArthritis beginning before age 16, lasting ≥6 weeks, after excluding other causes.
    OligoarticularYoung girls; ANA positivity increases risk of chronic anterior uveitis, which may be asymptomatic.
    SystemicQuotidian fever, evanescent salmon rash, arthritis and systemic inflammation; macrophage activation syndrome is a dangerous complication.
    Board pearlJIA-associated uveitis can be silent—screening is based on risk, not eye symptoms.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Rheumatology

    Acute rheumatic fever

    TriggerImmune-mediated disease after group A streptococcal pharyngitis.
    Major featuresMigratory polyarthritis, carditis, chorea, erythema marginatum and subcutaneous nodules.
    ImportantEvidence of preceding GAS infection supports the diagnosis; secondary antibiotic prophylaxis prevents recurrence.
    Board pearlA migratory arthritis or chorea weeks after strep throat should trigger the Jones-criteria framework.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Vasculitis

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Rheumatology

    IgA vasculitis

    TetralogyPalpable purpura (legs/buttocks), arthralgia/arthritis, abdominal pain and renal involvement.
    GI riskIntussusception can complicate severe abdominal involvement.
    Renal follow-upMonitor blood pressure and urinalysis because nephritis may appear after the rash.
    Board pearlPalpable purpura + abdominal pain + arthralgia in a child = IgA vasculitis.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Rheumatology

    Behçet disease

    PatternRecurrent oral aphthous ulcers plus genital ulcers, ocular inflammation/uveitis, and variable skin, vascular, neurologic, or articular disease.
    PathergyA pathergy test is positive when minor skin trauma produces an exaggerated papule/pustule; it supports the diagnosis but is not required.
    PopulationMore common along the historic Silk Road/Mediterranean-to-Asian regions, but it can occur in any population.
    Board pearl Recurrent oral + genital ulcers with uveitis is the classic triad; pathergy is a supporting clue.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Systemic autoimmune disease

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Rheumatology

    Systemic lupus erythematosus in children

    CommonConstitutional symptoms, photosensitive/malar rash, nonerosive arthritis, cytopenias and renal disease.
    AntibodiesANA is sensitive; anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith are more specific. Low complement can track active disease.
    RenalUrinalysis/proteinuria and renal function are central because lupus nephritis drives morbidity.
    Board pearlA positive ANA alone does not diagnose SLE; clinical context and specific antibodies matter.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Rheumatology

    Juvenile dermatomyositis

    WeaknessSymmetric proximal muscle weakness—difficulty climbing stairs, rising from the floor, or lifting arms.
    SkinHeliotrope rash and Gottron papules/sign are classic.
    OtherElevated muscle enzymes and MRI evidence of myositis support diagnosis; calcinosis is a notable pediatric complication.
    Board pearl Proximal weakness + heliotrope rash/Gottron papules = juvenile dermatomyositis.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Periodic fever

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Rheumatology

    Periodic fever: PFAPA pattern

    PatternRegularly recurrent fevers in a young child with aphthous ulcers, pharyngitis, and cervical adenitis.
    Between episodesChild is typically well with normal growth.
    PearlThe predictable periodicity and wellness between attacks help distinguish PFAPA from recurrent infections.
    Board pearl Clocklike fevers + aphthae + pharyngitis + adenitis in a thriving child is PFAPA.

    Eczematous & inflammatory dermatitis

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Dermatology

    Atopic dermatitis

    PatternPruritic chronic relapsing eczema; cheeks/extensor surfaces in infants, flexural predominance in older children.
    Treatment coreDaily emollients and topical anti-inflammatory therapy for flares; avoid unnecessary irritants.
    ComplicationEczema herpeticum causes monomorphic painful vesicles/erosions with systemic illness and requires urgent antiviral therapy.
    Board pearlThe symptom that defines atopic dermatitis is pruritus.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Dermatology

    Diaper dermatitis: irritant vs Candida

    IrritantErythema on convex surfaces with relative sparing of skin folds.
    CandidaBeefy red plaques involving folds with satellite papules/pustules.
    PearlPersistent diaper rash after antibiotics or with fold involvement should raise concern for Candida.
    Board pearl Fold sparing = irritant; fold involvement + satellites = Candida.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Bacterial skin disease

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Dermatology

    Impetigo vs staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome

    ImpetigoLocalized superficial infection; honey-colored crusts are classic. Bullous impetigo is toxin-mediated S aureus.
    SSSSDiffuse tenderness/erythema followed by superficial blistering/desquamation from exfoliative toxin; mucous membranes are typically spared.
    Board pearlMucosal sparing helps distinguish SSSS from Stevens-Johnson syndrome/TEN.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Dermatology

    Blistering distal dactylitis

    CauseMost often group A Streptococcus; S aureus can also cause it.
    LesionTense fluid-filled blister on an erythematous base over the volar distal finger pad.
    ContextYoung children, especially with atopic dermatitis or nail biting/picking; systemic symptoms and lymphangitis are usually absent.
    Board pearlA tense blister isolated to a distal finger pad is not classic bullous impetigo—think blistering distal dactylitis.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Fungal & parasitic infection

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Dermatology

    Tinea capitis

    PresentationScaly alopecic patches, broken hairs/“black dots,” lymphadenopathy, or an inflammatory kerion.
    TreatmentRequires systemic antifungal therapy because topical agents do not adequately penetrate the hair shaft.
    Board pearlScalp dermatophyte infection needs oral therapy.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Dermatology

    Scabies

    PatternIntensely pruritic eruption, often worse at night, with household contacts who may also itch.
    DistributionFinger webs, wrists, axillae, waistline, and genital region are common; infants can have scalp/palm/sole involvement.
    ClueBurrows are characteristic but may be hard to find.
    Board pearl Nocturnal itch in multiple household members is a major scabies clue.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Viral / benign lesions

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Dermatology

    Molluscum contagiosum

    LesionSmall, smooth, dome-shaped papules with central umbilication.
    CourseUsually self-limited in immunocompetent children.
    AssociationMore numerous/persistent lesions occur with atopic dermatitis or immunodeficiency.
    Board pearl Umbilicated pearly papules in a well child are molluscum until proven otherwise.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Vascular lesions

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Dermatology

    Infantile hemangioma

    CourseTypically appears in the first weeks of life, proliferates during infancy, then slowly involutes.
    Treat whenThreat to vision/airway, ulceration, high-output cardiac effects, or risk of permanent disfigurement/function loss.
    First lineOral propranolol is standard first-line therapy for problematic infantile hemangiomas.
    Board pearl Most hemangiomas can be observed; treat based on location, function, complications, and disfigurement risk—not size alone.

    Musculoskeletal

    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Hip disorders

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Musculoskeletal

    Developmental dysplasia of the hip

    Newborn examBarlow tests whether an unstable hip can be dislocated; Ortolani reduces a dislocated hip.
    ImagingUltrasound is preferred in young infants before femoral-head ossification; radiographs become more useful later.
    TreatmentPavlik harness is typical initial treatment in young infants; older/persistent cases may require reduction and casting or surgery.
    Board pearlOrtolani reduces; Barlow dislocates.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Musculoskeletal

    Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease

    WhoUsually younger school-age children, more often boys.
    PresentationInsidious limp and hip/groin or referred knee pain with limited abduction/internal rotation.
    MechanismIdiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral head.
    Board pearlSCFE is the heavier adolescent; Perthes is the younger child with avascular necrosis.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Musculoskeletal

    SCFE

    WhoTypically overweight adolescents; endocrine disorders such as hypothyroidism increase risk.
    PresentationHip/groin or referred knee pain, limp, out-toeing, and limited internal rotation.
    ActionMake the patient non–weight-bearing and obtain urgent orthopedic evaluation for surgical fixation.
    Board pearlObese adolescent with knee pain and limited hip internal rotation = SCFE until proven otherwise.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Musculoskeletal

    Septic arthritis vs transient synovitis

    Septic arthritisToxic/febrile child, severe pain with passive ROM, refusal to bear weight, inflammatory markers often high; urgent joint aspiration and antibiotics.
    Transient synovitisOften follows viral illness, child generally well appearing, lower inflammatory burden, self-limited.
    Board pearlA hot, exquisitely painful joint with systemic illness is septic arthritis until proven otherwise.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Bone infection

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Musculoskeletal

    Acute hematogenous osteomyelitis

    PresentationFever with focal bone pain/tenderness, limp, or refusal to use an extremity.
    OrganismStaphylococcus aureus is most common; special host/exposure clues modify the differential.
    ImagingMRI is the most sensitive imaging modality early when diagnosis remains uncertain.
    Board pearl A child who will not bear weight with focal metaphyseal tenderness and fever needs evaluation for osteomyelitis.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Overuse & common injuries

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Musculoskeletal

    Osgood-Schlatter disease

    WhoActive adolescent during a growth spurt.
    PainActivity-related anterior knee pain and tenderness/swelling at the tibial tubercle.
    TreatmentActivity modification, stretching/strengthening, ice, and analgesics; symptoms improve with skeletal maturity.
    Board pearl Tibial tubercle pain in a running/jumping adolescent is Osgood-Schlatter, not intra-articular knee disease.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Musculoskeletal

    Nursemaid elbow

    MechanismRadial head subluxation after axial traction on an extended/pronated arm, usually in a toddler.
    PositionChild holds the arm slightly flexed and pronated and refuses to use it, usually without swelling or deformity.
    TreatmentPrompt reduction; imaging is unnecessary when the history/exam are classic and there is no concern for fracture.
    Board pearl A toddler suddenly refusing to use an arm after a pull on the hand is nursemaid elbow.

    Ophthalmology & ENT

    6 snapshots · 1 comparisons · 185 unique facts
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Eye disease

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Ophthalmology & ENT

    Retinoblastoma

    PresentationLeukocoria or strabismus in a young child.
    GeneticsRB1 tumor-suppressor mutation on chromosome 13; bilateral/multifocal disease strongly suggests a germline mutation.
    Long-termHeritable disease increases risk of second malignancies, especially osteosarcoma.
    Board pearlLeukocoria is retinoblastoma until proven otherwise.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Ophthalmology & ENT

    Amblyopia and strabismus

    AmblyopiaReduced vision from abnormal visual development during a critical period, commonly due to strabismus, anisometropia, or deprivation.
    TreatmentCorrect the underlying optical problem and force use of the weaker eye with patching or pharmacologic penalization when indicated.
    UrgencyEarlier treatment is more effective because visual plasticity declines with age.
    Board pearl Strabismus is not just cosmetic—untreated misalignment can cause permanent amblyopia.
    COMPARE / CONTRAST

    Preseptal vs orbital cellulitis

    PreseptalEyelid erythema/swelling but normal vision, normal ocular motility, and no proptosis.
    OrbitalPain/restriction with eye movement, proptosis, decreased vision, afferent pupillary defect, or ophthalmoplegia.
    ActionOrbital signs require urgent imaging, IV antibiotics, and specialty evaluation.
    Painful/restricted extraocular movements are a major orbital red flag.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Ear & hearing

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Ophthalmology & ENT

    Acute otitis media

    DiagnosisBulging tympanic membrane or new otorrhea not due to otitis externa; middle-ear effusion plus acute inflammation is key.
    TreatmentAmoxicillin is usual first-line when antibiotics are indicated; selected mild cases can be observed depending on age/severity/laterality.
    Board pearlA red tympanic membrane alone does not diagnose AOM—look for bulging/effusion.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Ophthalmology & ENT

    Newborn hearing screen follow-up

    ScreenUniversal newborn hearing screening is performed early.
    Failed screenRequires diagnostic audiologic evaluation rather than repeated reassurance.
    Why it mattersEarly identification and intervention are critical for language development.
    Board pearl A failed newborn hearing screen is not “wait and see”; timely diagnostic audiology matters.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Sinus & deep-neck infection

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Ophthalmology & ENT

    Acute bacterial sinusitis

    PersistentURI symptoms lasting >10 days without improvement.
    SevereHigh fever with purulent nasal discharge for several consecutive days.
    WorseningNew fever, worsening discharge, or cough after initial improvement (“double sickening”).
    Board pearl Duration and trajectory—not green mucus alone—distinguish bacterial sinusitis from a viral URI.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Ophthalmology & ENT

    Deep neck infection: retropharyngeal vs peritonsillar

    Retropharyngeal abscessYounger child with fever, neck stiffness/torticollis, drooling, muffled voice, and possible respiratory distress.
    Peritonsillar abscessOlder child/adolescent with severe unilateral sore throat, trismus, muffled “hot-potato” voice, and uvular deviation.
    EmergencyAirway compromise requires immediate airway-focused management.
    Board pearl Torticollis favors retropharyngeal abscess; trismus + uvular deviation favors peritonsillar abscess.

    Behavior & Psychiatry

    5 snapshots · 1 comparisons · 108 unique facts
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Externalizing disorders

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Behavior & Psychiatry

    Oppositional defiant disorder

    PatternAngry/irritable mood, argumentative/defiant behavior and/or vindictiveness lasting at least 6 months with impairment.
    ThresholdAt least 4 symptoms during interaction with at least one person who is not a sibling.
    VindictivenessSpiteful/vindictive behavior on at least 2 occasions in the prior 6 months.
    DistinctionUnlike conduct disorder, ODD does not require serious aggression, property destruction, theft, or major rights violations.
    Board pearlODD is chronic defiance/irritability—not the severe rights violations of conduct disorder.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Behavior & Psychiatry

    ADHD: diagnostic frame

    CoreDevelopmentally inappropriate inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity causing impairment.
    SettingsSymptoms must be present in more than one setting and begin in childhood.
    Before labelingConsider sleep problems, learning disorders, anxiety/depression, hearing/vision problems, trauma, medications/substances and environmental mismatch.
    Board pearlSchool-only symptoms are not enough for ADHD; impairment must span settings.
    COMPARE / CONTRAST

    ODD vs conduct disorder vs ADHD

    ODDDefiance/argumentativeness/irritability without serious violation of others’ rights.
    Conduct disorderAggression, cruelty, destruction, theft/deceit, or serious rule violations.
    ADHDDevelopmentally inappropriate inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity across settings; behavior is not primarily spiteful or rights-violating.
    Ask what drives the behavior: attention/impulsivity, defiance, or serious rights violations.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Neurodevelopment

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Behavior & Psychiatry

    Autism spectrum disorder

    Core domainsPersistent social-communication/social-interaction deficits plus restricted/repetitive behaviors or interests.
    CluesPoor joint attention, reduced social reciprocity, delayed/atypical language, repetitive movements, insistence on sameness, unusual sensory responses.
    ActionDevelopmental evaluation and early intervention should not wait for a definitive etiologic diagnosis.
    Board pearlLoss of language/social skills or absent joint attention is a developmental red flag.

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Behavior & Psychiatry

    Depression and suicide risk in adolescents

    PresentationIrritability may substitute for depressed mood; look for anhedonia, sleep/appetite change, guilt/hopelessness, concentration problems, or functional decline.
    SafetyAny suicidal ideation requires direct assessment of intent, plan, access to lethal means, past attempts, and protective factors.
    UrgencyActive intent/plan, inability to maintain safety, severe agitation/psychosis, or lack of supervision warrants emergency evaluation.
    Board pearl Asking directly about suicide does not increase suicidal behavior and is necessary when risk is suspected.

    Tic disorders

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Behavior & Psychiatry

    Tic disorders and Tourette syndrome

    TicsSudden, rapid, recurrent motor movements or vocalizations that can be temporarily suppressed and often fluctuate.
    TouretteMultiple motor tics plus at least one vocal tic over a chronic course, with onset before adulthood.
    ComorbidityADHD and OCD symptoms are common and may cause more impairment than the tics themselves.
    Board pearl Treat the impairment, not the appearance of the tic—comorbid ADHD/OCD often drives morbidity.

    Emergency & Toxicology

    10 snapshots · 1 comparisons · 451 unique facts
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Medication & toxin exposures

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Emergency & Toxicology

    Acetaminophen overdose

    ToxicityExcess NAPQI depletes glutathione and causes hepatic injury.
    AssessmentFor an acute single ingestion, obtain a timed acetaminophen level and use the Rumack–Matthew nomogram when applicable.
    AntidoteN-acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione and is most effective when started early, but remains useful even with later presentation.
    Board pearlDo not wait for liver injury to start NAC when the history/level indicates treatment.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Emergency & Toxicology

    Salicylate toxicity

    EarlyRespiratory alkalosis from direct stimulation of the respiratory center.
    ProgressionAnion-gap metabolic acidosis develops; children may present predominantly acidotic.
    Treatment conceptVolume/glucose support and serum/urine alkalinization; severe toxicity may require hemodialysis.
    Board pearlA mixed respiratory alkalosis + anion-gap metabolic acidosis is the classic salicylate pattern.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Emergency & Toxicology

    Iron poisoning

    EarlySevere GI symptoms, hemorrhagic gastritis, shock and metabolic acidosis.
    LaterA transient apparent recovery can precede hepatic failure.
    AntidoteDeferoxamine for significant systemic toxicity/high-risk poisoning.
    Board pearlIron is a corrosive mitochondrial toxin; severe early GI illness is a warning sign.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Emergency & Toxicology

    Opioid poisoning

    ToxidromeCNS depression, respiratory depression, and miosis—although pupils are not always pinpoint.
    TreatmentAirway/ventilatory support plus naloxone when clinically indicated.
    PearlRecurrent respiratory depression can occur after naloxone when the opioid outlasts the antagonist.
    Board pearl Treat the respiratory depression; naloxone is a tool, not a substitute for ventilation.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Emergency & Toxicology

    Carbon monoxide poisoning

    SymptomsHeadache, dizziness, nausea, confusion, syncope, chest pain, or flu-like symptoms in multiple exposed people.
    DiagnosisCarboxyhemoglobin level supports diagnosis; routine pulse oximetry can appear falsely reassuring.
    TreatmentImmediate high-concentration oxygen; consider hyperbaric oxygen in severe poisoning or selected high-risk circumstances.
    Board pearl Several family members with “flu” symptoms plus a combustion exposure should trigger carbon monoxide testing.
    COMPARE / CONTRAST

    Toxidrome bedside compare

    OpioidCNS + respiratory depression, miosis.
    AnticholinergicAgitation/delirium, mydriasis, dry/flushed skin, urinary retention, decreased bowel sounds.
    SympathomimeticAgitation, mydriasis, tachycardia, hypertension, diaphoresis.
    Serotonin syndromeAgitation, autonomic instability, hyperreflexia and clonus, often GI hyperactivity.
    Dry vs sweaty and reflexes/clonus are especially useful toxidrome discriminators.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    High-risk ingestions

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Emergency & Toxicology

    Button battery ingestion

    DangerEsophageal batteries can cause liquefactive necrosis and deep tissue injury within hours.
    ActionAn esophageal button battery requires emergent removal.
    ClueOn radiograph, the “double halo”/step-off appearance helps distinguish a battery from a coin.
    Board pearlLocation matters: esophageal button battery = emergency.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Emergency & Toxicology

    Caustic ingestion

    Do notDo not induce emesis, neutralize the agent, or blindly place an NG tube.
    ConcernDrooling, dysphagia, oral burns, stridor, chest/abdominal pain or vomiting suggest significant injury.
    EvaluationAirway stabilization first; endoscopic assessment is used for significant exposures based on symptoms and toxicology/GI guidance.
    Board pearlThe mouth can look normal despite significant esophageal injury.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Envenomation & anaphylaxis

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Emergency & Toxicology

    Scorpion envenomation

    US speciesClinically important U.S. stings are usually Centruroides, especially the bark scorpion in the Southwest.
    NeuromuscularParesthesias, abnormal eye movements, dysphagia/drooling, slurred speech, tongue/extremity fasciculations or jerking.
    AutonomicTachycardia, diaphoresis, salivation, vomiting and bronchoconstriction can occur.
    Board pearlCranial-nerve dysfunction plus autonomic hyperactivity after a sting is the classic severe bark-scorpion pattern.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Emergency & Toxicology

    Anaphylaxis

    RecognizeAcute multisystem allergic reaction with airway/breathing compromise and/or hypotension; skin findings may be absent.
    First lineIM epinephrine in the lateral thigh—do not delay for antihistamines or steroids.
    AfterObserve according to severity/risk, prescribe epinephrine autoinjector when appropriate, and provide trigger avoidance/emergency education.
    Board pearl Epinephrine is first-line treatment for anaphylaxis; antihistamines are adjuncts.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Shock

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Emergency & Toxicology

    Pediatric shock: perfusion first

    EarlyTachycardia, delayed capillary refill, cool/mottled extremities, altered mental status, and decreased urine output.
    LateHypotension is a late and ominous finding in children.
    ApproachSupport airway/oxygenation, obtain access, give targeted fluid/blood products when appropriate, and treat the underlying cause while reassessing frequently.
    Board pearl A normotensive child can still be in shock—use perfusion and mental status, not blood pressure alone.

Additional fluid may be required. | Monitor conjunctival pH with litmus paper 10-20 min. after irrigation | consider ophtho consult and d/w poison control
    • Cervical spine and neck imaging → PECARN C-spine criteria, consider obtaining imaging if any of the following are present in a pt </= 16yo: | 1. AMS | 2. Focal neurologic deficits | 3. Complaint of neck pain | 4. Torticollis | 5. substantial injury to torso | 6. Predisposing condition | 7. High-risk MVC | 8. Diving accident | many institutions use NEXUS criteria for clinical c-spine clearance. This is validated in children >/= 8yo and includes #1, 2, and 3 of PECARN c-spine rules plus presence of intoxication or painful, distracting injury | Recent guidelines by Pediatric Cervical Spine Clearance Working Group Algorithm additionally highlight the following factors: | a. in pts </= 3 yo, consider plain radiographs, if c-spine cannot be cleared clinically | b. clinical clearance can be done regardless of MOI if child is >/= 3 yo and is asx with normal mental status and normal PE | c. Clinical clearance CANNOT be performed if child is observed to have or reports persistent neck pain, OR if there is abnormal head posture or difficulty in neck movement

    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Diagnostic test performance

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Ethics & Biostatistics

    Diagnostic test characteristics

    SensitivityProbability the test is positive when disease is present; high sensitivity means few false negatives.
    SpecificityProbability the test is negative when disease is absent; high specificity means few false positives.
    PrevalenceSensitivity/specificity are intrinsic test characteristics; positive and negative predictive values change with disease prevalence.
    Board pearl High sensitivity helps rule out when negative; high specificity helps rule in when positive—when the clinical context supports using the test that way.
    COMPARE / CONTRAST

    Test characteristics: what changes with prevalence?

    Sensitivity / specificityDo not depend on disease prevalence in the tested population.
    Positive predictive valueRises as prevalence/pretest probability rises.
    Negative predictive valueFalls as prevalence/pretest probability rises.
    Prevalence changes predictive values, not sensitivity or specificity.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Statistical inference & analysis

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Ethics & Biostatistics

    Type I vs type II error

    Type I / αFalse positive: conclude there is a difference/effect when none truly exists.
    Type II / βFalse negative: fail to detect a real difference/effect.
    Power1 − β; increasing sample size generally improves power and reduces type II error risk.
    Board pearl Type I = false alarm; Type II = missed real effect.
    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Ethics & Biostatistics

    Intention-to-treat analysis

    RuleAnalyze participants in the groups to which they were originally randomized, regardless of adherence/crossover.
    WhyPreserves the benefits of randomization and better reflects real-world effectiveness.
    ContrastPer-protocol analyses can estimate efficacy among adherent participants but are more vulnerable to bias.
    Board pearl Intention-to-treat protects randomization; it does not mean ignoring outcomes or missing data.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Consent, assent & confidentiality

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Ethics & Biostatistics

    Consent, assent, and adolescent confidentiality

    PermissionParents/guardians generally provide permission for minors except where law allows minors to consent independently.
    AssentDevelopmentally capable children/adolescents should be involved in decisions and provide assent when appropriate.
    ConfidentialityPrivate adolescent care is important, but safety threats, suspected abuse, and mandatory-reporting situations override confidentiality.
    Board pearl Pediatric decision-making is usually parent permission + child assent, with increasing respect for adolescent autonomy.

    Pharmacokinetics

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Pharmacology

    First-order vs zero-order elimination

    First orderA constant fraction of drug is eliminated per unit time; most drugs follow this pattern over usual concentrations.
    Zero orderA constant amount is eliminated per unit time after metabolic pathways become saturated.
    PearlSteady state for a first-order drug is reached after roughly 4–5 half-lives.
    Board pearl First order = fraction per time; zero order = fixed amount per time.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Sedation & procedural medication safety

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Pharmacology

    Pre-sedation fasting: practical framework

    Clear liquidsShortest fasting interval.
    Breast milkLonger than clear liquids but shorter than formula/solid foods.
    Solids/fatty mealsRequire the longest fasting interval before elective sedation/anesthesia.
    Board pearl Aspiration risk rises with heavier gastric contents; exact fasting intervals should follow the current anesthesia/sedation protocol.
    CLINICAL CLUSTER

    Medication toxicity

    SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Pharmacology

    Serotonin syndrome: medication toxicity pattern

    PatternAgitation, autonomic hyperactivity, hyperthermia, diarrhea, tremor, hyperreflexia, and clonus after serotonergic exposure.
    ContrastClonus/hyperreflexia favor serotonin syndrome over anticholinergic toxicity or neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
    TreatmentStop serotonergic agents, provide supportive care/benzodiazepines, and use serotonin antagonism such as cyproheptadine in selected cases.
    Board pearl Clonus is one of the most useful bedside clues to serotonin syndrome.

      Diagnostic-test research

      SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Epidemiology

      ROC curves

      AxesPlots sensitivity (true-positive rate) against 1 − specificity (false-positive rate) across test thresholds.
      Best cornerUpper left represents high sensitivity and high specificity.
      AUCLarger area under the curve indicates better overall discrimination.
      Board pearl Moving the cutoff trades sensitivity for specificity; the ROC curve visualizes that tradeoff.
      SYNTHESIZED SNAPSHOT · Epidemiology

      Study design for a diagnostic test

      Core ideaCompare the index test with a reference standard in a relevant patient population.
      Typical designCross-sectional diagnostic-accuracy studies are commonly used because disease status and test performance are assessed in the same clinical sample.
      Avoid biasSpectrum, selection, and verification bias can markedly distort apparent test performance.
      Board pearl A diagnostic test is judged against a reference standard—not simply by whether outcomes improve.
